name: Bicuspid Aortic Valve
description: Two leaflets instead of three on the aortic valve. Leads to stenosis, regurgitation, and aortic root dilation over decades; often asymptomatic until adulthood.

frequency.sources: Siu & Silversides, JACC 2010; BAV prevalence 1–2% all ages

diagnosis: Echocardiography (TTE/TEE); CT/MRI for aortic sizing. Often incidentally found.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surveillance echocardiography until
intervention thresholds met. Surgical valve
repair or replacement; Ross procedure
preferred in children and young adults.
TAVR for adult patients with suitable
anatomy and prior surgical/biological failure.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter valve-in-valve
TAVR for failed bioprostheses;
NOTCH1/ROBO4 genotype-guided aortic
surveillance protocols; aortic root remodeling
techniques to delay replacement.

name: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
description: Hole in the wall separating the two lower chambers. Blood shunts left to right, overloading the lungs. Small VSDs often close spontaneously.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; Liu et al., IJE 2019; 3–4/1,000 live births

diagnosis: Echocardiography. Prenatal fetal echo. Cardiac catheterization for complex cases.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Observation for small VSDs (70–80%
close spontaneously). Surgical patch closure
for large or symptomatic VSDs.
Transcatheter device closure for muscular
VSDs (Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter perimembranous
VSD closure: Lifetech KONAR-MF device
(CE-marked; US trials ongoing).
Perventricular hybrid muscular VSD closure
via mini-sternotomy.

name: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
description: Hole in the wall separating the upper chambers. Low- pressure shunt causes right heart enlargement and eventual pulmonary hypertension if untreated.

frequency.sources: Liu et al., IJE 2019; ~1– 2/1,000 live births; prevalence increased 6-fold with echo era

diagnosis: Echocardiography (TTE/TEE). Bubble study for PFO differentiation. Cardiac MRI for complex anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare: Transcatheter device closure (Amplatzer Septal Occluder, Gore Cardioform) for secundum ASDs — >80% of cases. Surgical closure for primum, sinus venosus, or complex defects.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter closure of sinus
venosus ASDs with partial anomalous
pulmonary venous return (Gore ASSURED
device — US pivotal trial completed).
Fenestrated closure devices for borderline
pulmonary hypertension.

name: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)
description: Fetal vessel connecting pulmonary artery to aorta fails to close after birth. Blood shunts aorta to pulmonary, overloading lungs.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; 1/2,000 full- term births; ~70% of infants <28 wks

diagnosis: Echocardiography; continuous murmur, bounding pulses, widened pulse pressure.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Indomethacin or ibuprofen (medical
closure, 70–80% in premature infants).
Transcatheter closure: Amplatzer Piccolo
Occluder (FDA 2019, down to 700g) for
hemodynamically significant PDAs. Surgical
ligation for refractory cases.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Acetaminophen as alternative
medical closure agent. Catheter-based
closure in extremely premature infants <1 kg
at specialized centers.
Conservative/expectant management
strategies for very premature infants gaining
evidence.

name: Pulmonary Stenosis
description: Narrowing at the pulmonary valve or surrounding structures. Three subtypes: (1) Valvar PS (90%); (2) Subvalvar/Infundibular PS -- muscular/fibrous obstruction, requires surgical resection; (3) Supravalvar/Branch PA stenosis -- associated with Williams, Noonan, Alagille syndromes.

frequency.sources: Liu et al., IJE 2019; ~8/10,000 births; 8–10% of all CHD

diagnosis: Echo with Doppler gradient (distinguish valvar, subvalvar, supravalvar). Cardiac catheterization for intervention planning. CT/MRI for complex anatomy or supravalvar disease.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Valvar PS: balloon valvuloplasty for
gradient >40 mmHg (>90% success).
Surgical repair for dysplastic valves (Noonan
syndrome). Subvalvar PS: surgical
resection. Branch PA stenosis: transcatheter
balloon dilation and stenting.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:TPVR (Melody, SAPIEN 3,
Harmony TPV) for RVOT dysfunction post-
repair. MEK inhibitor therapy (trametinib) for
Noonan-associated RASopathy PS/HCM
(FDA Breakthrough Designation).

name: Coarctation of the Aorta
description: Focal narrowing of the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery. Creates two-zone circulation: HTN upper body, hypotension below.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; 4–6/10,000 births; males 2×

diagnosis: Echo, CT angiography, or MRI. BP differential between arms and legs is pathognomonic.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Neonates: surgical resection with end-
to-end anastomosis. Older children/adults:
transcatheter balloon dilation ± stenting
(covered stents preferred). Prostaglandin E1
to maintain ductal patency in critical
neonatal coarctation.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Covered stent technology (Gore
Viabahn, NuMED CP stent) for de novo and
recurrent coarctation reducing aneurysm
risk. Surveillance MRI protocols for long-
term aortopathy after repair.

name: Atrioventricular Septal Defect (AVSD)
description: Combined atrial + ventricular hole with malformation of the central heart valves. Associated with Down syndrome in 40-50% of cases.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; ~3/10,000 births; Down syndrome in ~60% of AVSD cases

diagnosis: Echocardiography. AVSD AI detection app available. Fetal echo for prenatal diagnosis.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Complete surgical repair (double-patch
closure of both ASD and VSD + AV valve
reconstruction) in first 3–6 months of life.
Pre-operative management of pulmonary
hypertension.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Improved surgical techniques for
common AV valve reconstruction; refined
timing protocols for partial vs. complete
forms. Transcatheter AV valve repair
(MitraClip, PASCAL) for recurrent post-
operative MR in adults.

name: Partial AVSD (Primum ASD)
description: Incomplete form: only the atrial component present - - primum ASD in inferior atrial septum adjacent to AV valves -- without ventricular septal component. AV valves abnormal (left AV valve cleft causing MR) but no inlet VSD. Often misclassified as simple ASD; mitral valve pathology and surgical approach are fundamentally different.

frequency.sources: Partial AVSD ~1–2/10,000 births; ~30% of all AVSDs; Down syndrome in ~20%

diagnosis: Echo: primum ASD in inferior septum abutting AV valves; left AV valve cleft on short-axis; assess MR severity. Cardiac MRI. Catheterization for pulmonary pressure if MR severe or delayed presentation.

treatment.standardOfCare: Surgical repair: primum ASD closure + direct suture closure of left AV valve cleft. Timing: 3–6 months if significant MR; defer to 1–2 years if mild. Operative mortality <1% at experienced centers. Lifelong surveillance; late MR recurrence ~5–10%.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter AV valve repair (MitraClip) for recurrent post-repair MR in
adult patients not suitable for reoperation.

name: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
description: Four defects: large VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, RV hypertrophy. Most common cyanotic CHD. Virtually all post-repair patients require lifelong follow-up for residual PR, RV dilation, and arrhythmia. Variant: TOF with Absent PV Syndrome (~3-5%) -- massive free PR with aneurysmal PA dilation compressing mainstem bronchi.

frequency.us: and Europe. US: ~1,080–2,160 new/yr; ~350,000 US total (children + adults with repaired TOF)
frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; 3–6/10,000 births; 22q11 deletion in ~15%

diagnosis: Echocardiography. Cardiac MRI -- gold standard post-repair: RVEDVi >150-160 mL/m2 = PVR threshold. ECG: QRS >180 ms = independent SCD predictor. Holter. CT for absent PV variant PA anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Complete intracardiac repair (VSD
closure + RVOT enlargement/transannular
patch) in first year. Post-repair PVR when
RVEDVi >150 mL/m² or RVEF <47%. TPVR:
Melody (conduit), SAPIEN 3 (conduit/native
RVOT), Harmony TPV (native RVOT, FDA
2021). ICD for VT/VF risk.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Expanded Harmony TPV22
indications for dilated native RVOT. Earlier
PVR timing trials to prevent RV dysfunction.
TOF with atretic PV: PA reduction plasty +
VSD closure + valved conduit. RVOT
substrate ablation for refractory VT.

name: D-Transposition of Great Arteries (D-TGA)
description: Aorta and pulmonary artery are switched -- oxygenated and deoxygenated blood circulate in parallel. Cardiac emergency at birth.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; 3–5/10,000 births; males 2–3:1

diagnosis: Fetal echocardiography. Pulse oximetry screening at birth. Urgent echo for cyanotic newborn.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Prostaglandin E1 to maintain PDA.
Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind
procedure, bedside echo guidance) when
atrial communication restrictive — life-
saving. Arterial switch operation (ASO)
within first 2 weeks of life.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Refined coronary reimplantation
techniques for complex coronary anatomy
patterns. Long-term neoaortic root
surveillance protocols post-ASO; earlier
intervention thresholds for neoaortic root
dilation.

name: Congenital Aortic Stenosis
description: Narrowing of the aortic valve present from birth. Critical neonatal form causes cardiogenic shock when ductus closes.
diagnosis: Echocardiography. Fetal echo for prenatal diagnosis. Cardiac catheterization for intervention planning.

treatment.standardOfCare: Balloon valvuloplasty (acute success

name: Supravalvar Aortic Stenosis (SVAS)
description: Fixed obstruction of ascending aorta at/above sinotubular junction. Two forms: (1) Williams syndrome-associated (~75%) -- ELN deletion 7q11.23, bilateral PA stenosis co-exists; (2) Isolated/non-syndromic (~25%) -- ELN point mutations. Critical: commissures may adhere to supra-aortic ridge, obstructing coronary ostia and risking coronary ischemia -- mandatory intraoperative assessment. Doty three- patch aortoplasty (inverted Y incision, three patch inserts) is technique of choice.

frequency.us: ~180–360 isolated SVAS cases/yr; ~720– 1,080 Williams- related cases/yr
frequency.sources: Morris et al., Pediatrics 2010; Williams syndrome 1/7,500–10,000 births; SVAS in ~75% of Williams

diagnosis: Echo: gradient across sinotubular junction; bilateral PA pressures; coronary origins. CT/MRI: full anatomy of ascending aorta, arch, branch PAs, and coronary ostia relative to ridge. Cardiac catheterization: pressure gradient; coronary angiography if coronary ischemia suspected. FISH/CMA for 7q11.23 if Williams suspected.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical repair indicated for gradient
>50 mmHg, symptoms, or LV dysfunction.
Doty three-patch aortoplasty preferred.
Inspect coronary ostia for ridge adherence at
operation. Branch PA stenosis: transcatheter
stenting. Lifelong surveillance
echocardiography.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter approaches for
discrete membranous SVAS. Elastin-
targeted therapies for Williams syndrome-
related arteriopathy (preclinical). Coronary
ostial protection techniques to reduce
perioperative SCD risk.

name: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS)
description: Entire left side of heart severely underdeveloped. RV must support both pulmonary and systemic circulation. Most severe CHD.

frequency.sources: CDC/CHOP; HLHS 2–3/10,000 births; 25–40% of cardiac deaths in week 1 of life

diagnosis: Fetal echo (often 18-24 wks). Postnatal: echo, CT/MRI. Assess atrial septum size -- restrictive atrial septum (~5-10% of HLHS) carries significantly higher operative mortality.

treatment.standardOfCare: Prostaglandin E1 emergently. Balloon/stent atrial septostomy for restrictive atrial septum. Three-stage Norwood/Glenn/Fontan palliation or Hybrid Norwood. Interstage home pulse oximetry monitoring (reduces interstage mortality from ~15% to ~2–5%). Cardiac transplantation for selected patients.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Fetal cardiac intervention (balloon aortic valvuloplasty) for borderline HLHS to promote LV growth. Stem cell
therapy (cardiosphere-derived cells —
TICAP, PERSEUS trials). Ventricular
recruitment strategies. Improved Fontan
outcomes with fenestration and thoracic
lymphatic interventions.

name: Ebstein's Anomaly
description: Tricuspid valve leaflets displaced downward into RV, 'atrializing' a portion of it. Associated WPW in 25- 30%.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; 1/20,000 births; wide severity spectrum

diagnosis: Echocardiography. ECG for WPW. Cardiac MRI for RV function.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Cone procedure (valve reconstruction
using native leaflet tissue) — procedure of
choice. ICD for WPW/arrhythmia risk.
Catheter ablation for accessory pathway.
Bidirectional Glenn shunt for severe RV
dysfunction.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter tricuspid valve
interventions (CLASP TR, FORMA, TriClip)
for patients with residual TR not suitable for
reoperation. Refined Cone technique
outcomes driving earlier surgical referral.

name: Truncus Arteriosus
description: Single great vessel exits the heart instead of two. Complete mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; 1/10,000 births; 22q11 deletion in ~35%

diagnosis: Echocardiography; fetal echo for prenatal diagnosis. Catheterization for pulmonary artery anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare: Surgical repair in neonatal period: VSD closure, separation of pulmonary arteries, RV-to-PA conduit placement. TPVR (Melody/SAPIEN 3/Harmony TPV) for conduit failure — defers or replaces surgical reintervention. Branch PA stenosis: catheter balloon dilation and stenting.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Tissue-engineered conduits (decellularized homografts, bioresorbable scaffolds) under investigation to reduce reintervention burden. Expanding transcatheter pulmonary valve options for native/dilated RVOT.

name: Interrupted Aortic Arch
description: Complete discontinuity of the aortic arch. Survival depends on PDA; cardiovascular collapse when ductus closes. Associated with 22q11 deletion in 50-70%.
diagnosis: Fetal/neonatal echocardiography. CT angiography for arch anatomy. Genetic testing for 22q11 deletion.

treatment.standardOfCare: Prostaglandin E1 emergently. Surgical arch reconstruction connecting arch segments + simultaneous VSD closure.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Hybrid and staged approaches for high-risk neonates. Transcatheter management of recurrent arch obstruction post-repair. Genotype-guided counseling for 22q11.2 deletion (~50% of IAA).

name: Pulmonary Vein Disease (TAPVR/PAPVR)
description: Pulmonary veins drain anomalously -- not into left atrium. Obstructed forms are neonatal emergencies. Post-surgical pulmonary vein stenosis is a distinct, aggressive complication.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; TAPVR 1– 2/10,000 births; ~2% of CHD

diagnosis: Echocardiography. CT/MRI for drainage anatomy. Fetal echo for complex forms.

treatment.standardOfCare: Urgent surgical repair for obstructed TAPVR (emergency). Elective repair in first weeks/months for unobstructed TAPVR. Sutureless repair technique reduces post- surgical PV stenosis risk. Serial echo surveillance every 3–6 months for ≥2 years post-repair.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Sutureless 'pericardium-in-situ' technique refinements for reoperations. Systemic antifibrotic therapy (sirolimus, imatinib) for post-operative PV stenosis — active trials. Drug-eluting balloon for transcatheter treatment of stenotic repaired veins.

name: Double Outlet Right Ventricle (DORV)
description: Both great arteries arise from the RV. Four distinct surgical diagnoses by VSD position: (1) Subaortic VSD -- LV-to- aorta tunnel; (2) Subpulmonary VSD (Taussig-Bing) -- arterial switch; (3) Doubly- committed VSD -- tunnel repair; (4) Remote VSD -- often Fontan palliation. Incorrect anatomic classification leads to the wrong operation.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; DORV 1– 2/10,000 births; Taussig-Bing ~15% of DORV

diagnosis: Echocardiography. Cardiac MRI -- essential for VSD position, great artery relationships, and coronary anatomy. Catheterization for pulmonary pressure assessment. 3D reconstruction for surgical planning.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgery individualized by VSD location
and great artery relationship: intraventricular
LV-to-aorta tunnel (REV or Rastelli) for
subaortic VSD; arterial switch + VSD closure
(Taussig-Bing); staged Fontan for remote
VSD or complex anatomy.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:3D printing and computational
flow modeling for pre-operative surgical
planning in complex DORV. Hybrid
strategies for high-risk neonates. No single
DORV repair strategy exists — anatomy
determines operation.

name: Double Inlet Left Ventricle (DILV)
description: Both atria connect to a single dominant left ventricle; RV absent or hypoplastic. Classic single-ventricle anatomy.

frequency.sources: DILV

diagnosis: Echocardiography. Cardiac catheterization before Fontan (includes APC mapping and embolization).

treatment.standardOfCare: Staged Fontan palliation (bidirectional Glenn → Fontan). Pre-Fontan catheterization: APC embolization (present in ~50–70% at Glenn stage). Heart transplantation for Fontan failure.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Thoracic lymphatic embolization for Fontan-related PLE and plastic bronchitis. Combined heart-liver

name: L-Transposition (L-TGA / ccTGA)
description: Both AV and VA connections discordant -- 'physiologically corrected' but morphologic RV supports systemic circulation it was not designed for.

frequency.sources: L-TGA ~1/33,000 births; <1% of CHD; congenitally corrected TGA

diagnosis: Echocardiography. ECG for heart block (develops ~2%/year). Cardiac MRI for RV function tracking.

treatment.standardOfCare: Observation if no associated defects and systemic RV function preserved. Double-switch operation (atrial switch + ASO or REV) to restore LV to systemic position. Permanent pacemaker for complete heart block.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Timing optimization for double- switch based on LV retraining protocols. Transcatheter approaches for associated lesions (VSD device closure, PS balloon dilation). Long-term systemic RV failure surveillance driving earlier double-switch referral.

name: Pulmonary Atresia with Intact VS (PA-IVS)
description: Atretic (imperforate) pulmonary valve with intact septum; RV develops without normal outflow. RV-dependent coronary circulation in 30- 50%.

frequency.sources: PA-IVS ~1/10,000 births; ~1% of CHD; spectrum from mild to severe RV hypoplasia

diagnosis: Echocardiography. Cardiac catheterization essential to assess coronary anatomy. Fetal echo.

treatment.standardOfCare: Prostaglandin E1. RF perforation + balloon valvuloplasty for adequate RV (biventricular pathway if RV grows). Biventricular or single-ventricle (Fontan) pathway determined by RV size, tricuspid valve annulus z-score, and coronary anatomy (RVDCC).
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Fetal cardiac intervention (in utero pulmonary valvuloplasty) to promote RV growth and potentially avoid univentricular palliation. Refined RV suitability criteria for biventricular vs. one- and-a-half ventricle repair.

name: Pulmonary Atresia with VSD and MAPCAs
description: Atretic pulmonary valve + hypoplastic/absent pulmonary arteries; lungs supplied by major aortopulmonary collateral arteries (MAPCAs). Catheter-based MAPCA mapping and embolization is a core part of management.

frequency.sources: PA/VSD/MAPCAs ~1–2/10,000 births; complete repair feasible in ~60–70%

diagnosis: Echocardiography. CT angiography essential for MAPCA mapping. Catheterization for pressure assessment and collateral anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare: Unifocalization surgery (consolidating all MAPCAs into one PA system) + complete intracardiac repair. Multiple staged operations and catheter reinterventions anticipated. Catheter-based MAPCA occlusion for non-unifocalized collaterals causing overcirculation.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:One-stage complete unifocalization + repair (Hanley approach, Stanford) demonstrating improved outcomes over staged repair. Improved conduit options and TPVR to defer surgical reintervention. CT angiography with 3D reconstruction for MAPCA mapping.

name: Tricuspid Atresia
description: Complete absence of tricuspid valve; absent/hypoplastic RV. Left ventricle functions as the sole pump after Fontan palliation.

frequency.sources: van der Linde et al., JACC 2011; tricuspid atresia 1–2/10,000 births; 1–3% of CHD

diagnosis: Echocardiography. Cardiac catheterization before Fontan (hemodynamics, APC mapping, PA pressure assessment). Fetal echo.

treatment.standardOfCare: Staged Fontan palliation (BT shunt → bidirectional Glenn → Fontan). Pre-Fontan catheterization: APC coil embolization, branch PA stenting if needed. Post-Fontan serial catheterizations for APC surveillance and Fontan pathway assessment.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Fontan optimization with fenestration and thoracic lymphatic embolization for PLE/plastic bronchitis. Mechanical cavopulmonary assist devices (TCPC pump) under investigation. Heart transplantation remains definitive for Fontan failure.

name: Shone's Complex
description: Four left-sided obstructive lesions: supravalvar mitral ring, parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis, and coarctation of aorta.

frequency.sources: Shone 1963; <1/100,000 births; 4 left-sided obstructive lesions as defining spectrum

diagnosis: Echocardiography (serial). Cardiac catheterization for hemodynamics. CT/MRI for aortic anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Staged surgical relief at each
obstructive level (supramitral ring, parachute
MV, aortic valve, coarctation). Transcatheter
balloon dilation ± stenting of coarctation as
bridge or primary treatment. High
reintervention rates expected; lifelong
surveillance.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter mitral interventions
(balloon dilation of supramitral ring, MitraClip
for residual MR). Tissue-engineered valves
for mitral replacement in growing children
(avoiding anticoagulation).

name: Congenital Mitral Valve Anomalies
description: Spectrum: (1) Parachute Mitral Valve -- all chordae to single papillary muscle; functional MS; part of Shone's complex; (2) Double Orifice Mitral Valve -- two orifices separated by fibrous bridge; (3) Isolated Mitral Leaflet Cleft -- cleft without AVSD; (4) Mitral Atresia -- part of HLHS/single-ventricle spectrum.

frequency.sources: Congenital MS ~0.5–1/10,000 births; parachute MV <1/100,000; often part of Shone complex

diagnosis: Echocardiography (2D and 3D TEE essential for subtype distinction and surgical planning). Cardiac MRI for ventricular function. Catheterization for pulmonary pressure. Fetal echo.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Repair preferred over replacement in
children. Isolated mitral cleft: direct suture
closure (>90% success). Parachute MV and
double-orifice MV: repair tailored to
dominant anatomy; replacement often
ultimately required. Mitral atresia: Fontan
palliation.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter mitral valve repair
(MitraClip, PASCAL) for recurrent MR post-
surgical repair in adolescents/adults. Tissue-
engineered and expandable mitral
prostheses to accommodate somatic growth.

name: Aortic Arch Abnormalities (Vascular Rings)
description: Developmental anomalies of aortic arch including double arch, right arch with aberrant subclavian, cervical arch. Vascular rings encircle trachea/esophagus.

frequency.sources: Vascular rings ~1–3% of CHD; double aortic arch 40–60% of complete rings

diagnosis: Echocardiography. CT angiography gold standard for ring anatomy. Bronchoscopy for tracheomalacia.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical ring division (ligating minor
arch/ligamentum arteriosum). Excellent
outcomes at experienced centers.
Tracheobronchomalacia managed with
airway stenting or aortopexy if persistent
post-ring division.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Thoracoscopic (minimally
invasive) ring division — comparable
outcomes to open surgery with faster
recovery. Pre-operative 3D CT
reconstruction and virtual surgical planning
for complex double aortic arch.

name: ALCAPA
description: Left coronary artery arises from the pulmonary artery rather than the aorta, causing myocardial ischemia from birth. Presents with infantile heart failure or sudden death.

frequency.sources: ALCAPA ~1/300,000 births; accounts for ~5% of infant cardiac deaths if unrepaired

diagnosis: Echocardiography (retrograde coronary flow on Doppler). CT coronary angiography. ECG may show anterolateral ischemia.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical coronary reimplantation
(transfer to aorta) — curative if performed
early. ECMO for hemodynamic instability. LV
function often recovers substantially with
unloading and revascularization.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Improved post-operative LV
recovery monitoring with cardiac MRI.
Ventricular assist devices as bridge to
recovery. Myocardial viability MRI to guide
expectation of LV functional recovery.

name: AAOCA (Anomalous Aortic Origin of Coronary Artery)
description: Coronary artery arises from the wrong sinus or follows an interarterial course between aorta and pulmonary artery. Risk of sudden cardiac death, especially with exertion.

frequency.sources: Davis et al., JACC 2016; AAOCA ~0.1–0.3% of general population

diagnosis: Echocardiography (limited). CT coronary angiography -- gold standard. Exercise stress testing for ischemia.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical unroofing of interarterial
segment (preferred for high-risk anatomy).
Exercise restriction pre-operatively.
Coronary reimplantation or bypass in select
cases.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Risk stratification protocols (FFR-
CT, stress perfusion MRI, exercise stress
echo) to refine surgical indications and
identify truly flow-limiting lesions. Watchful
waiting evidence expanding for low-risk
anatomy.

name: Heterotaxy Syndrome / Atrial Isomerism
description: Abnormal left-right organ arrangement combined with complex intracardiac defects. Right isomerism (asplenia) associated with severe cyanotic CHD; left isomerism (polysplenia) with heart block and interrupted IVC.

frequency.sources: Heterotaxy ~1–2/10,000 births; ~3% of CHD; right isomerism ~50–70% mortality without intervention

diagnosis: Fetal/neonatal echocardiography. CT/MRI for cardiac and visceral situs. Abdominal ultrasound for spleen. Genetic testing. ECG for heart block.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Highly individualized: most require
staged Fontan palliation. Asplenia: lifelong
penicillin prophylaxis ±
pneumococcal/meningococcal vaccines.
Pacemaker for complete heart block (left
isomerism).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Improved AV valve repair
strategies for complex heterotaxy valve
anatomy. Bilateral SVC management
optimization. Liver laterality assessment for
equitable hepatic flow distribution in Fontan.
Lymphatic interventions for post-Fontan
complications.

name: Aortopulmonary Window
description: Rare communication between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery, distinct from PDA. Causes massive left-to- right shunting and neonatal heart failure.

frequency.sources: Aortopulmonary window ~1/100,000 births; <1% of CHD

diagnosis: Echocardiography. CT angiography for anatomy. Cardiac catheterization for pulmonary vascular resistance.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical repair (direct closure or patch)
in neonatal period. Transcatheter device
closure for suitable anatomy (distant from
coronary ostia and pulmonary valves).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Expanded catheter-based
closure with Amplatzer Duct Occluder II and
custom devices for AP windows with suitable
anatomy.

name: Cor Triatriatum
description: A fibromuscular membrane divides the left atrium into two chambers, creating pulmonary venous obstruction mimicking mitral stenosis.

frequency.sources: Cor triatriatum ~0.1– 0.4% of CHD; fibromuscular membrane obstructing left atrium

diagnosis: Echocardiography (TTE/TEE: membrane in left atrium with gradient). Cardiac MRI for complex anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare: Surgical membrane resection — curative in nearly all cases. Excellent outcomes with early repair before pulmonary hypertension develops.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Transcatheter balloon membrane dilation or perforation as bridge to surgery in high-risk neonates with obstructed cor triatriatum (very rare). Robot-assisted minimally invasive resection at specialized centers.

name: Discrete Subaortic Stenosis
description: Fibromuscular membrane or ridge immediately below the aortic valve in the LVOT causing fixed subvalvar obstruction. Progressive obstruction damages the aortic valve leaflets from the turbulent jet (causing AR). Recurrence after surgical resection ~10-20%. Strong male predominance.

frequency.sources: DSS ~1/30,000 births; ~15–20% of all LVOT obstruction; fibromuscular ridge may form post-birth

diagnosis: Echo: subvalvar membrane with peak LVOT gradient; assess aortic valve for secondary AR. Cardiac MRI: LVOT anatomy. Catheterization: LVOT pressure pullback. TEE for precise membrane localization.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical membrane resection ± septal
myectomy for gradient >30–40 mmHg or any
developing AR. Balloon dilation ineffective.
Post-op surveillance every 1–2 years
lifelong; 10–20% recurrence rate. AV
repair/replacement if secondary AR severe.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Earlier surgical intervention
protocols to prevent progressive AR —
intervention before AR becomes significant.
Cardiac MRI tissue characterization to
distinguish fibrous vs. muscular/tunnel LVOT
obstruction for surgical planning.

name: Sinus of Valsalva Aneurysm
description: Congenital aneurysm of an aortic sinus (right coronary ~70%; non- coronary ~25%). Rupture causes acute left-to-right shunt, continuous murmur, rapid heart failure, and hemodynamic collapse. Right coronary sinus aneurysm ruptures most commonly into the RV. Associated with VSD in ~30-50% of cases.

frequency.sources: Sinus of Valsalva aneurysm ~0.09% of CHD; ~1/100,000; predominantly right coronary sinus

diagnosis: Echo (TTE/TEE): aneurysmal sac; Doppler continuous high-velocity shunt on rupture. CT angiography: gold standard for anatomy. Cardiac catheterization: Qp/Qs, coronary anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical patch closure from both aortic
root and receiving cardiac chamber
simultaneously; associated VSD closed at
same operation. Emergency surgery for
acute rupture with hemodynamic instability.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter device closure
(Amplatzer Duct Occluder, Vascular Plug)
for suitable non-ruptured anatomy.
Endovascular stent-graft for selected high-
surgical-risk patients.

name: Scimitar Syndrome (Pulmonary Venolobar Syndrome)
description: Rare anomaly: entire right lung drains via large venous channel (the 'scimitar vein') into IVC rather than left atrium. Also includes: right lung hypoplasia and sequestration, dextroposition of heart, and in ~30% an aberrant systemic arterial supply to the right lower lobe. Distinct from TAPVR: involves only right lung, includes pulmonary hypoplasia, requires different surgical approach.

frequency.sources: Scimitar syndrome ~1– 3/100,000 births; female predominance 2:1

diagnosis: Chest X-ray: pathognomonic 'scimitar sign' -- curvilinear density paralleling right heart border. CT angiography: gold standard -- scimitar vein course, drainage site, anomalous aortic supply, right lung hypoplasia. Echo. Cardiac catheterization: PVR, selective aortography for anomalous arterial supply.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical redirection of scimitar vein to
left atrium via intra-atrial baffle or direct
reimplantation; concurrent ligation of
aberrant aortic arteries. Observation for mild
asymptomatic adult forms (Qp/Qs <1.5).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter baffle creation with
stent-based redirection of scimitar vein
(avoids cardiopulmonary bypass in selected
cases). Combined embolization of aberrant
aortic collaterals + transcatheter venous
redirection.

name: Unroofed Coronary Sinus / PLSVC Draining to Left Atrium
description: Congenital absence of roof of coronary sinus creating communication with left atrium. Underlying anatomy: PLSVC drains into coronary sinus which then drains into LA, causing right-to-left shunt and cyanosis. Classic missed diagnosis at ASD repair: patching the ASD without recognizing unroofed coronary sinus causes persistent post- operative cyanosis. PLSVC itself (~3-10% of CHD) is usually benign but must be identified before any cardiac operation.

frequency.us: ~1% of all CHD. PLSVC: ~3- 10% of CHD overall; ~0.3% of general population. Complete unroofing: ~0.1% of CHD. US: ~720–3,600 new cases/yr (PLSVC + unroofed CS combined); ~25,000–75,000 US total
frequency.sources: PLSVC ~3– 10% of CHD; unroofed coronary sinus ~1% of CHD; often clinically silent FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Echo: dilated coronary sinus; bubble contrast study -- microbubbles appear in LA from left arm injection (diagnostic for PLSVC-to-LA drainage). CT angiography: gold standard for PLSVC anatomy and coronary sinus continuity. Cardiac catheterization: O2 saturation step-up/step- down; selective venography.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical repair: (1) PLSVC ligation if
right SVC present and bridging vein
adequate + coronary sinus closure; (2)
Baffling to redirect flow to RA; (3) PLSVC
reimplantation to RA appendage if no right
SVC. Pre-operative identification mandatory
before any cardiac surgery.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Transcatheter occlusion of
PLSVC in selected adult patients with
adequate collateral drainage. Identification
protocols (routine pre-op echo screening) to
prevent inadvertent PLSVC ligation.

name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)
description: Abnormal LV wall thickening from sarcomere gene mutations. Obstructive form (HOCM) causes outflow obstruction. Leading cause of sudden death in young athletes.

frequency.us: ~1,460,000 US total all ages; ~200,000–300,000 US pediatric/adolescent
frequency.sources: Maron et al., JACC 2022; HCM ~1/500 individuals; ~700,000 Americans

diagnosis: Echocardiography (septal thickness >=15mm or >=13mm with family history). Genetic testing. CMR for fibrosis (LGE). ECG screening.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Beta blockers, calcium channel
blockers for symptom management. Septal
myectomy (surgical gold standard for
refractory LVOTO). Alcohol septal ablation
for appropriate anatomy. ICD for high-risk
patients (SCD prevention).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Mavacamten (Camzyos, FDA
2022) — cardiac myosin inhibitor; first
disease-modifying drug for obstructive HCM.
Aficamten (Myqorzo, FDA 2025) — next-
generation myosin inhibitor. Expanding use
in pediatric/adolescent populations.

name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)
description: LV (and often both ventricles) dilated with impaired contractility. Most common cardiomyopathy requiring pediatric transplantation.

frequency.us: ~200–400 new pediatric cases/yr; ~5,000–10,000 US pediatric prevalent
frequency.sources: Towbin et al., Circulation 2006; pediatric DCM 0.57– 1.13/100,000 children/yr

diagnosis: Echocardiography (LVEF <55%, LV dilation). Cardiac MRI. Genetic panel. Endomyocardial biopsy if myocarditis suspected.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta blockers,
diuretics, aldosterone antagonists.
Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) for pediatric
HF (FDA-approved ≥1 year). CRT for
dyssynchrony. ICD. VAD as bridge to
transplantation (Berlin Heart EXCOR <15
kg; continuous-flow for larger). Cardiac
transplantation.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin,
empagliflozin) expanding to pediatric HF
with emerging evidence. Gene therapy for
genetic DCM subtypes (LMNA, TTN,
RBM20) in early trials. Precision medicine
genotype-guided therapy.

name: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCM)
description: Stiff, non-compliant ventricles with elevated filling pressures. Systolic function initially preserved. Rarest and worst- prognosis pediatric cardiomyopathy.

frequency.us: ~22–29 new pediatric cases/yr; ~500–1,000 US pediatric prevalent
frequency.sources: Colan et al., JACC 2007; RCM 0.03–0.04/100,000 children/yr; 2–5% of pediatric CMs

diagnosis: Echocardiography (biatrial enlargement, normal LV size/EF, restrictive filling pattern). Cardiac MRI. Cardiac catheterization.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Diuretics for symptomatic relief only.
Cardiac transplantation is the only effective
long-term treatment; early listing is standard
practice.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:mTOR pathway modulation for
sarcomeric RCM. Gene therapy targeting
MYH7, TNNI3 variants under investigation.
Refined transplant listing criteria to optimize
timing.

name: ARVC (Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy)
description: Genetically defined (desmosomal gene mutations: PKP2, DSP, DSG2) cardiomyopathy with fibro-fatty replacement of RV myocardium. Causes ventricular arrhythmias triggered by exercise; leading cause of SCD in young athletes.

frequency.us: ~14,600– 36,500 US total all ages; ~3,000–7,000 US pediatric
frequency.sources: Corrado et al., Circulation 2017; ARVC ~1/2,000– 5,000; PKP2 most common mutation

diagnosis: Task Force Criteria (revised 2020). Cardiac MRI (fibro-fatty infiltration, RV dilation, RVEF). ECG: epsilon waves, T-wave inversions V1-V3. Holter. Exercise stress test. Genetic panel (desmosomal genes). Endomyocardial biopsy.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Exercise restriction — critical and
mandatory. ICD for sustained VT, VF, or
syncope. Catheter ablation for refractory VT
(epicardial approach often required). Beta
blockers. Heart transplantation for advanced
biventricular failure.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Flecainide as add-on
antiarrhythmic therapy. Gene-silencing
approaches (ASO, siRNA) for PKP2
pathogenic variants in preclinical
development. Sports cardiology risk
stratification refinements for risk-stratified
return-to-play decisions.

name: Left Ventricular Non- Compaction (LVNC)
description: Distinct cardiomyopathy characterized by prominent trabeculations and a non-compacted inner myocardial layer. Associated with multiple genetic mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3, LMNA, TAZ). Causes heart failure, ventricular arrhythmias, and thromboembolic risk.

frequency.sources: Towbin et al., JACC 2022; echocardiographic prevalence 0.05– 0.24%; significant diagnostic variability between Jenni and Petersen criteria

diagnosis: Echo: Jenni criteria (NC/C ratio >2 in adults, >1.4 in children in systole). Cardiac MRI. Genetic panel. ECG (LBBB, WPW pattern).

treatment.standardOfCare: Standard heart failure therapy (ACEi/ARB, beta blocker, diuretics). Anticoagulation for LVEF <35% or thrombus. ICD for high-risk arrhythmia. Cardiac transplantation for refractory HF.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Genetic phenotype-specific management — reclassification of
pathological vs. physiological non-
compaction using refined MRI criteria
(NCC/CC ratio, strain imaging). Emerging
evidence that isolated LVNC may not require
therapy without LV dysfunction.

name: Duchenne MD Cardiomyopathy
description: Progressive dilated cardiomyopathy from dystrophin gene mutations. Cardiac involvement is nearly universal by age 18; now the leading cause of DMD death.

frequency.us: ~1,000–1,400 new US male cases/yr; ~75,000– 100,000 US Duchenne total
frequency.sources: Hoffman et al., NEJM 2019; DMD 1/3,500–5,000 male births; cardiomyopathy present virtually all by age 18

diagnosis: Annual echocardiography + ECG from age 10 (or at diagnosis). Cardiac MRI with LGE for early fibrosis detection. LVEF monitoring.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ACE inhibitors (cardioprotective even
pre-dysfunction — start by age 10). Beta
blockers once cardiac dysfunction present.
Corticosteroids (deflazacort preferred).
Ventilatory support. ICD consideration for
arrhythmia.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Delandistrogene moxeparvovec
(Elevidys, Sarepta, FDA 2023/2024) —
micro-dystrophin gene therapy for
ambulatory patients ≥4 years. Exon-skipping
therapies (eteplirsen, golodirsen, viltolarsen,
casimersen) for applicable mutations.
Givinostat (HDAC inhibitor, FDA 2024) for
muscle and cardiac preservation.

name: Emery-Dreifuss MD / LMNA Cardiomyopathy
description: Caused by LMNA or EMD gene mutations. Classic triad: early joint contractures, slowly progressive muscular dystrophy, and life- threatening cardiac conduction disease progressing to DCM. Highest SCD risk of any inherited condition.

frequency.sources: Emery- Dreifuss MD ~1/100,000; LMNA cardiac disease SCD risk >5%/yr without ICD

diagnosis: ECG: atrial standstill, progressive heart block (pathognomonic for EDMD). Echocardiography (DCM). Holter for conduction disease and VT. Genetic testing (LMNA, EMD).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Early and aggressive ICD implantation — mainstay even before significant DCM (LMNA mutations carry very high sudden death risk). Pacemaker for symptomatic bradycardia/heart block. Standard HF therapy. Cardiac transplantation for
advanced disease.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Temsirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) in
early trials for LMNA-DCM. SGLT2 inhibitors
for laminopathy-associated HF. Gene
therapy for LMNA haploinsufficiency in
preclinical stage.

name: Myocarditis
description: Inflammation of heart muscle, most commonly viral (enterovirus, adenovirus, parvovirus B19). Ranges from mild to fulminant cardiogenic shock.

frequency.us: ~200–400 new US pediatric clinical cases/yr (true incidence ~5× higher)
frequency.sources: Freedman et al., Circulation 2016; myocarditis ~1–2/100,000 children/yr; significantly underdiagnosed

diagnosis: Echo (LV dysfunction). Cardiac MRI (gold standard: T2 edema, LGE fibrosis, Lake Louise criteria). Endomyocardial biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Supportive care. MCS: ECMO as
rescue for fulminant cardiogenic shock; VAD
(Berlin Heart EXCOR <15 kg or continuous-
flow for larger) as bridge to recovery or
transplantation. Immunosuppression for
giant cell/eosinophilic/autoimmune
myocarditis. Heart transplantation.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Endomyocardial biopsy-guided
and cardiac MRI-guided immunosuppression
protocols (corticosteroids + azathioprine for
lymphocytic myocarditis per updated
European guidelines). Anakinra (IL-1
antagonist) for immune-mediated
myocarditis with hemodynamic compromise.
Pembrolizumab discontinuation +
corticosteroids for immune checkpoint
inhibitor myocarditis.

name: Pompe Disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II)
description: Autosomal recessive lysosomal acid alpha- glucosidase (GAA) deficiency. Classic infantile form: massive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + hypotonia + respiratory failure within first year.

frequency.us: ~26–52 new US infantile cases/yr; ~90 new US all- forms cases/yr
frequency.sources: van Capelle et al., Orphanet 2016; classic infantile Pompe ~1/138,000 births; all forms ~1/40,000

diagnosis: Newborn screening (GAA enzyme activity). GAA enzyme assay in leukocytes. GAA gene sequencing. Echo (massive HCM). ECG (giant QRS complexes, shortened PR interval). CK elevation.

treatment.standardOfCare: ERT: alglucosidase alfa (Myozyme/Lumizyme, Sanofi) — initiate as early as possible; cardiac function often normalizes with early treatment. Respiratory support. Newborn screening allows pre- symptomatic treatment.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Next-generation ERT: cipaglucosidase alfa + miglustat (Pombiliti + Opfolda, Amicus, FDA 2023) — improved glycan-independent cellular uptake, superior to alglucosidase alfa in late-onset disease.
Gene therapy: AAV-based approaches
(AT845, Spark Therapeutics) in Phase 1/2
trials. mRNA replacement therapy under
investigation.

name: Danon Disease
description: X-linked lysosomal storage disorder (LAMP2 gene mutations). Classic triad: HCM, skeletal myopathy, and intellectual disability. WPW syndrome in ~70% of males. Rapidly progressive HCM often requiring transplantation.

frequency.us: ~180–360 US total all ages; ~50– 100 US pediatric cases
frequency.sources: Danon disease ~1/40,000; X-linked LAMP2 mutation; ~1% of HCM referrals

diagnosis: Echo (severe HCM, often massive). ECG: WPW pattern, extremely high voltage. Lysosomal enzyme panel (LAMP2 protein absent on immunostaining). Genetic testing (LAMP2). Muscle biopsy. Cardiac MRI (LGE fibrosis).

treatment.standardOfCare:
ICD for SCD risk (combination of WPW
+ severe HCM). Catheter ablation for WPW
accessory pathway. Cardiac transplantation
— often the only effective long-term therapy;
median age at transplantation ~20 years in
males.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Gene therapy: AT845 (Astellas,
AAV9-LAMP2B) in Phase 1/2 trials —
promising early results for LAMP2 protein
restoration. Female carriers require close
cardiac surveillance (later-onset, variable
penetrance).

name: Fabry Disease (Cardiac)
description: Lysosomal storage disorder (alpha- galactosidase A deficiency). Cardiac manifestations: HCM, arrhythmia, heart failure.

frequency.us: ~1,800–8,700 US total (including late-onset variants); ~500–1,000 US pediatric
frequency.global: ~70,000– 340,000 global (all ages, including late- onset variants)
frequency.sources: Mehta et al., Genet Med 2020; classical Fabry ~1/40,000; NBS studies suggest ~1/3,100 including late-onset variants

diagnosis: Enzyme activity (alpha-gal A) in leukocytes. Genetic testing. Echo and cardiac MRI. Plasma/urine Gb3. Newborn screening in some states.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ERT: agalsidase alfa (Replagal, EU) or
agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme, Sanofi, US).
Treat cardiac complications: beta
blockers/CCBs for HCM, anticoagulation for
stroke risk, ICD/pacemaker for arrhythmia
and heart block.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Migalastat (Galafold, Amicus) —
oral pharmacological chaperone for patients
with amenable GLA mutations (~35–50% of
patients); non-inferior to ERT. Next-
generation ERT: pegunigalsidase alfa (PRX-
102, Chiesi, EU approved) for superior
stability and reduced immunogenicity. Gene
therapy trials: ST-920 (4D Molecular
Therapeutics), 4D-310 in Phase 1/2.

name: Friedreich's Ataxia (Cardiac)
description: GAA repeat expansion in frataxin gene causes mitochondrial iron accumulation. Cardiac involvement (HCM + arrhythmia) present in >90% and is the leading cause of death.

frequency.us: ~730–1,460 US total with cardiac involvement; ~500– 1,000 US pediatric
frequency.sources: Durr, Lancet Neurol 2010; Friedreich's ataxia ~1/50,000; HCM in ~80% of patients

diagnosis: Echocardiography (LV hypertrophy). Cardiac MRI. ECG (T-wave inversion common). Genetic testing (GAA repeat length).

treatment.standardOfCare: Beta blockers for symptomatic HCM. ACE inhibitors for heart failure. ICD consideration for malignant arrhythmia/sustained VT. Cardiac surveillance annual echo + ECG.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Omaveloxolone (Skyclarys, FDA 2023) — first disease-modifying therapy for FA (age ≥16); reduces neurological progression; cardiac effects under prospective evaluation. Frataxin replacement: mRNA therapy (Larimar, CTI- 1601) in Phase 2; AAV-FXN gene therapy in early Phase 1. Epigenetic reactivation of silenced frataxin allele (HDAC inhibitors).

name: Barth Syndrome (Cardiac)
description: X-linked disorder (tafazzin gene mutations) with abnormal cardiolipin metabolism. Presents with DCM, skeletal myopathy, neutropenia, and growth retardation.

frequency.us: ~9–12 new US male cases/yr; ~200–500 US total
frequency.sources: Barth Syndrome Foundation; ~1/300,000– 400,000 male births; X-linked TAZ mutation; significantly underdiagnosed

diagnosis: Echocardiography (DCM; occasionally non- compaction). Urine 3- methylglutaconic acid. Plasma/urine monolysocardiolipin ratio. Genetic testing (TAZ gene).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Standard HF therapy (ACE inhibitors,
beta blockers, diuretics). Nutritional support
(leucine supplementation). ICD for
ventricular arrhythmia. Cardiac
transplantation for refractory HF.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Elamipretide (SS-31,
mitochondria-targeted peptide, Stealth
BioTherapeutics) — Phase 2 trial in Barth
syndrome (TAZPOWER trial). TAZ gene
therapy (AAV-mediated tafazzin restoration)
in preclinical stage.

name: Mucopolysaccharidoses (Cardiac)
description: Lysosomal storage disorders (MPS I/Hurler, MPS II/Hunter, MPS IVA/Morquio, MPS VI) causing progressive glycosaminoglycan accumulation in cardiac valves, coronary arteries, and myocardium.

frequency.us: ~120–144 new US cases/yr (all MPS combined); ~10,000–20,000 US total
frequency.sources: Khan et al., Orphanet 2017; combined MPS ~1/25,000–30,000 births; cardiac valvular involvement in virtually all MPS types

diagnosis: Echocardiography (serial: valve thickening, regurgitation/stenosis progression). Urine glycosaminoglycans. Leukocyte enzyme activity assay. Genetic testing.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ERT: laronidase (MPS I/Aldurazyme), idursulfase (MPS II/Elaprase), galsulfase (MPS VI/Naglazyme), elosulfase alfa (MPS IVA/Vimizim). HSCT for MPS I Hurler before age 2.5 years (prevents cognitive decline, cardiac benefit partial). Surgical valve repair/replacement for advanced valve
disease.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Intrathecal/intracerebroventricular
ERT to address CNS disease (not reached
by IV ERT). Gene therapy: in vivo AAV and
ex vivo HSCT-gene therapy combinations
for MPS I, II, III (active Phase 1/2 trials).
Substrate reduction therapy (SRT) with
genistein, miglustat. Genome editing (ZFN,
CRISPR) preclinical.

name: Mitochondrial Cardiomyopathy
description: Cardiomyopathy (most commonly HCM, less commonly DCM) caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins -- failure of oxidative phosphorylation in energy- demanding cardiomyocytes. Major syndromes: MELAS, Kearns-Sayre (complete heart block + HCM), Leigh syndrome (severe infantile HCM), MERRF. Unlike sarcomeric HCM, myectomy and septal reduction are rarely appropriate. Cardiac transplantation is controversial because multisystem disease continues after transplant.

frequency.us: ~730–1,460 new US cases/yr; ~12,000–24,000 US total with cardiac involvement
frequency.sources: Mitochondrial disease ~1/5,000– 10,000; cardiac involvement in ~20– 40% of cases FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Echo: HCM pattern most common. ECG: complete heart block, pre-excitation, or conduction defects (especially KSS). Serum and CSF lactate (elevated). Muscle biopsy: ragged red fibers. Mitochondrial DNA sequencing; nuclear gene panel. Brain MRI (Leigh: symmetric basal ganglia T2 hyperintensities).

treatment.standardOfCare:
No disease-modifying therapy proven
to alter cardiac course. Standard HF
therapy. Mandatory pacemaker for complete
heart block (KSS — sudden death is a
leading cause). ICD for sustained VT/VF.
CoQ10 supplementation (widely used).
Avoid valproate (complex I inhibitor).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:NAD+ precursors (nicotinamide
riboside, NMN) under investigation.
Vatiquinone (EPI-743) in pediatric
mitochondrial disease trials. Idebenone for
LHON-related mitochondrial disease.
Mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT,
'three-parent IVF') for maternal inheritance
prevention — approved in UK, in use
clinically. Cardiac transplantation after
careful multidisciplinary review; multisystem
disease progression continues post-
transplant.

name: Marfan Syndrome (Cardiac)
description: Autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder (FBN1 gene). Cardinal cardiac features: progressive aortic root dilation (risk of dissection and rupture), aortic valve regurgitation, and mitral valve prolapse.

frequency.sources: De Paepe et al., Am J Med Genet 1996; Marfan ~1/5,000; ~65,000 Americans confirmed

diagnosis: Ghent criteria 2010. Echocardiography (aortic root Z-score). Annual cardiac MRI/CT. Slit-lamp exam (ectopia lentis). Genetic testing (FBN1). Family screening.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Losartan or atenolol — reduce aortic
root growth rate. Prophylactic aortic root
replacement when root >4.5–5.0 cm (or
aortic size index >2.75 cm/m²). Valve-
sparing root repair preferred in young
patients. Exercise restriction. Annual
echocardiographic surveillance.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:TGF-β pathway inhibitors beyond
losartan under investigation. Combined
ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) for Marfan-
associated LV dysfunction. FBN1 genotype-
specific surgical thresholds; aortic size index
and growth rate algorithms replacing
absolute diameter alone.

name: Loeys-Dietz Syndrome
description: Autosomal dominant aortopathy (TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, TGFB2/3 mutations). More aggressive aortic dilation and dissection at smaller diameters than Marfan syndrome.

frequency.sources: Loeys-Dietz syndrome ~1/50,000–100,000; TGFBR1/2, SMAD2/3, TGFB2/3 mutations

diagnosis: Genetic testing (TGFBR1/2, SMAD3, TGFB2/3 panel). Echocardiography. Full aortic MRI/CT from head to pelvis -- LDS affects entire arterial tree. Annual surveillance imaging.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Losartan — first-line therapy. Lower
threshold for prophylactic aortic surgery
(~4.0–4.5 cm vs. 5.0 cm in Marfan). Pan-
arterial surveillance (head-to-pelvis MRA
annually). Exercise restriction.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Genotype-specific thresholds:
TGFBR1 vs. TGFBR2 vs. SMAD3 vs.
TGFB2 variants have differing natural
histories. Targeted TGFBR pathway
inhibitors under investigation. Cervical artery
surveillance protocols standardizing.

name: Turner Syndrome (Cardiac)
description: Sex chromosome aneuploidy (45,X or mosaic). Cardiac findings in ~30-50%: bicuspid aortic valve (~16%), coarctation (~10%), aortic dilation. Dissection risk 6- 10x higher than general population despite relatively modest aortic dilation.

frequency.us: ~29,000– 36,500 new US cases/yr (all Turner); ~12,000– 18,000 cardiac cases/yr
frequency.sources: Turner syndrome ~1/2,000–2,500 live female births; BAV in ~30–50%; CoA in ~15%

diagnosis: Echocardiography at diagnosis (BAV, coarctation). MRI/CT for full aortic assessment. BP in all four extremities. Karyotype. Aortic size index (ASI) -- dissection risk increases significantly at ASI >2.5 cm/m2.

treatment.standardOfCare: Estrogen replacement therapy (starting ~12 years for puberty induction). Antihypertensive therapy. Prophylactic aortic surgery at lower thresholds than general population (ASI >2.5 cm/m²). Coarctation repair per standard protocols. Lifelong cardiology surveillance.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Refined aortic size index thresholds incorporating aortic area/height index. Growth hormone effects on aortic dimensions under study. Reproductive planning with high-risk obstetric centers for
those attempting pregnancy.

name: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS Type IV)
description: Autosomal dominant (COL3A1 mutations encoding type III procollagen). Most life- threatening EDS subtype. Unlike Marfan/Loeys- Dietz, the aortic root is often normal -- danger lies in spontaneous rupture of medium-sized arteries WITHOUT preceding aneurysm. Arterial tissue is extraordinarily fragile; sutures tear through native vessels. Operating on an undiagnosed vascular EDS patient is a recognized cause of intraoperative catastrophe.

frequency.us: EDS subtype: median survival ~48 years. First major complication by age 40 in ~80%. Arterial rupture is most common cause of death. US: ~730–2,920 US total; ~100–400 US pediatric
frequency.sources: Vascular EDS ~1/50,000– 200,000; COL3A1 mutations; median survival ~48 years FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Genetic testing (COL3A1 sequencing): gold standard. CT angiography of entire arterial tree: baseline mapping. MRI/MRA preferred over invasive angiography -- arterial puncture can cause uncontrollable hemorrhage. Echo: aortic root and valve. Avoid invasive arterial procedures unless absolutely necessary.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Conservative management strongly
preferred — avoid elective surgery.
Celiprolol (beta blocker with vasodilatory
properties) — only agent with RCT evidence
for reducing arterial event rates (BBEST
trial). Surgical intervention for life-
threatening rupture using modified technique
(pledgeted sutures, Teflon felt, minimal
tissue handling); endovascular preferred
over open. Pre-operative COL3A1 screening
before all vascular/cardiac surgery.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Losartan and irbesartan trials
ongoing. Improved endovascular techniques
for arterial complications (covered stents,
fenestrated grafts). Genetic counseling:
pregnancy carries very high risk (managed
at specialized centers with MFM + cardiac).

name: Takayasu Arteritis
description: Large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and major branches (subclavian, carotid, renal, mesenteric, coronary arteries). Predominantly affects adolescent girls. Causes progressive arterial stenosis, occlusion, and aneurysm formation. Cardiac complications: aortic regurgitation, coronary ostial stenosis, renovascular hypertension, limb ischemia. Critically: in the active inflammatory phase, surgical intervention carries very high restenosis rates -- surgery must be deferred until disease is in remission.

frequency.us: ~100–200 new US pediatric cases/yr; ~1,000– 2,000 US total
frequency.sources: Takayasu arteritis ~1– 2/million/yr overall; ~10–15% onset in childhood

diagnosis: Clinical: absent or diminished pulses, limb BP differential >10 mmHg, bruits, renovascular hypertension. Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, IL-6). CT angiography or MRA: vessel wall thickening, stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm -- gold standard. PET-CT: detects active vessel wall inflammation -- key for determining readiness for surgery. Echo: AR severity, coronary ostia.

treatment.standardOfCare: High-dose corticosteroids for active disease. Steroid-sparing agents: methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil. Surgical/endovascular intervention reserved for burnt-out disease in remission (PET-CT confirmed). Bypass grafting preferred over angioplasty for surgical revascularization.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) — best evidence for
refractory/steroid-dependent pediatric
Takayasu (used off-label in pediatrics; FDA-
approved for adult GCA). TNF inhibitors
(infliximab, adalimumab). Abatacept under
investigation. PET-CT standardization for
disease activity monitoring.

name: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH)
description: Intrinsic pulmonary vascular disease causing progressive arterial obliteration, elevated PA pressures, and right heart failure. Idiopathic or associated with CHD.

frequency.us: ~1,095–3,650 US pediatric cases; ~5,000–10,000 US total PAH all ages
frequency.sources: Simonneau et al., JACC 2019; idiopathic PAH 15– 50/million; pediatric PAH 0.7–4.4/million children/yr

diagnosis: Right heart catheterization (gold standard: mPAP >=25 mmHg, PVR >=3 Wood units). Echo. V/Q scan. Genetic testing (BMPR2). 6-minute walk test.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Targeted combination therapy: ERAs
(bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan) + PDE-
5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) ±
prostanoids (epoprostenol IV, treprostinil
SC/inhaled/IV, iloprost inhaled). Calcium
channel blockers for vasoreactive patients
(acute vasoreactivity testing-guided). Lung
or heart-lung transplantation for refractory
disease.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Sotatercept (Winrevair, Merck,
FDA 2024) — activin signaling inhibitor (anti-
ActRIIA); landmark STELLAR trial showed
significant reduction in PVR and 6MWD;
rapidly becoming add-on SOC. Ralinepag
(oral IP receptor agonist) in Phase 3. AAV-
BMPR2 gene therapy in preclinical
development.

name: Eisenmenger Syndrome
description: End-stage consequence of large unrepaired left-to- right shunt in which chronically elevated pulmonary blood flow produces irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease. Pulmonary vascular resistance rises until it exceeds systemic, causing right-to-left shunting and systemic cyanosis. Once established, cardiac repair is permanently and absolutely contraindicated -- closing the defect removes the 'pop-off valve' and causes acute right heart failure and death. A preventable disease: develops only when a surgically correctable defect is not repaired in time.

frequency.us: ~73–660 US total (markedly declined post-CHD repair era)
frequency.sources: Beghetti & Galie, Eur Heart J 2009; prevalence ~1–9/million in high- income countries now

diagnosis: Clinical: central cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia, reduced exercise tolerance, hemoptysis. Echo: bidirectional or right-to-left shunt flow; severe RV hypertension; RV hypertrophy and dilation. Right heart catheterization (essential): quantify PVR; vasodilator testing (negative in Eisenmenger). CT pulmonary angiography. CBC: polycythemia (Hct often 55-75%).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Cardiac repair absolutely contraindicated once Eisenmenger physiology established. PAH therapy (palliative): bosentan (best Eisenmenger RCT evidence), macitentan, sildenafil, tadalafil; prostanoids for advanced disease. Phlebotomy only for severe hyperviscosity (Hct >65%). Avoid: pregnancy (maternal mortality 30–50%), dehydration, high altitude, iron deficiency. Heart-lung
transplantation for selected deteriorating
patients.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Sotatercept (Winrevair): SuMILE
trial in Eisenmenger ongoing — anticipated
to shift management paradigm. Macitentan +
tadalafil combination trials. Riociguat (sGC
stimulator) has been used off-label in
Eisenmenger with some evidence.

name: Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH)
description: Mutations in both LDL receptor gene copies cause inability to clear LDL. Aggressive atherosclerosis from childhood; MI before age 20 without treatment.

frequency.us: patients. US: ~330–1,100 US total HoFH; ~2,000– 5,000 including milder FH
frequency.sources: Goldberg et al., JACC 2022; HoFH ~1/300,000– 1,000,000; LDL >400–500 mg/dL from birth FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Lipid panel (LDL 400- 1,000+ mg/dL). Genetic testing (LDLR, APOB, PCSK9). Carotid/coronary imaging. Vascular ultrasound.

treatment.standardOfCare:
High-intensity statins + ezetimibe +
PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab).
LDL apheresis every 1–2 weeks. Lomitapide
(MTP inhibitor) for HoFH.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Evinacumab (Evkeeza,
Regeneron, FDA 2021) — ANGPTL3
inhibitor; approved for HoFH ≥12 years;
significant LDL reduction independent of
LDL receptor function. Inclisiran (siRNA,
Leqvio) — trials ongoing for HoFH. LDL
receptor gene therapy (Phase 1/2 trials).

name: Long QT Syndrome (LQTS)
description: Inherited ion channel disorder causing prolonged cardiac repolarization and risk of torsades de pointes, syncope, and sudden cardiac death. Over 17 genetic subtypes; LQTS1 and LQTS2 account for >90% of genotyped cases.

frequency.sources: Schwartz et al., Circulation 2012; LQTS ~1/2,000 individuals; ~3,500 US sudden deaths/yr attributed to LQTS

diagnosis: 12-lead ECG (QTc >=480ms diagnostic; 460- 480ms borderline). Genetic panel. Exercise stress test. Schwartz score. Family screening.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Beta blockers (nadolol or propranolol
preferred over metoprolol) — first-line for all
LQTS types. ICD for high-risk patients
(cardiac arrest survivors, recurrent syncope
on therapy). Avoidance of QT-prolonging
medications. Activity restriction by genotype
(LQT1 most vulnerable to exercise, LQT2 to
auditory triggers).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Mexiletine add-on for LQTS3
(late sodium current blocker — reduces QTc
and events; now established practice). Left
cardiac sympathetic denervation (LCSD) for
refractory patients or those unable to
tolerate ICD. Gene therapy and
pharmacogenomic therapy for specific
KCNQ1/KCNH2 variants in preclinical
development.

name: CPVT (Catecholaminergic Polymorphic VT)
description: Rare inherited channelopathy (RYR2 or CASQ2 mutations) causing bidirectional or polymorphic VT during adrenergic stimulation. Structurally normal heart. SCD is often the first manifestation.

frequency.sources: Priori et al., Circulation 2002; CPVT ~1/10,000; RYR2 mutations in ~60–70% of cases

diagnosis: Exercise stress test or epinephrine provocation -- characteristic bidirectional or polymorphic VT. Normal resting ECG and echo. Genetic testing (RYR2, CASQ2). Family screening.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Nadolol (preferred beta blocker —
highest efficacy in CPVT). Flecainide add-on
(reduces VT burden significantly —
established adjunctive therapy). ICD for
survivors of cardiac arrest or breakthrough
VT/VF on therapy. Strict exercise restriction.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Left cardiac sympathetic
denervation (LCSD) — reduces ICD shocks
and VT episodes as adjunctive therapy.
RyR2-targeted stabilizers (dantrolene,
flecainide). Gene silencing of RYR2 gain-of-
function variants using ASO/siRNA —
preclinical.

name: Brugada Syndrome
description: Sodium channelopathy (SCN5A mutations in ~20- 30%) causing distinctive ECG pattern and risk of ventricular fibrillation, predominantly during rest or sleep. Structurally normal heart.

frequency.sources: Antzelevitch et al., Circulation 2005; Brugada ~1/2,000 globally; higher prevalence in SE Asia

diagnosis: Type 1 Brugada ECG pattern (coved ST elevation >=2mm in V1- V2) -- spontaneous or sodium channel blocker- provoked. Genetic testing (SCN5A). Fever management critical.

treatment.standardOfCare: ICD — only proven therapy for symptomatic patients (VF survivors, spontaneous sustained VT). Quinidine for electrical storm, VF storms, or ICD-ineligible patients. Aggressive fever management (antipyretics). Avoidance of sodium channel- blocking drugs.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) preferred in younger patients without pacing
indication. Epicardial ablation of the RVOT
arrhythmogenic substrate (Brugada hotspot
— Haïssaguerre protocol) — potentially
curative in specialized centers. Sodium
channel gain-of-function research guiding
novel pharmacology.

name: Short QT Syndrome (SQTS)
description: Rare inherited channelopathy characterized by pathologically shortened cardiac repolarization (QTc <320-340ms) and risk of ventricular fibrillation and SCD. Caused by gain-of- function mutations in potassium channel genes (KCNQ1, KCNH2, KCNJ2 -- the opposite mutations from LQTS). SCA or VF may be the first manifestation, including in infants. Critically distinct from LQTS: opposite pathophysiology; beta blockers used in LQTS are ineffective or potentially harmful in SQTS.

frequency.sources: Gollob et al., JACC 2011; SQTS <1/10,000; gain-of-function mutations in KCNH2, KCNQ1, KCNJ2 FREQUENCY

diagnosis: 12-lead ECG: QTc <320ms (definitive); 320- 340ms (borderline). Note: QT may appear near- normal at fast heart rates because QT does not shorten appropriately with rate increase (abnormal QT-RR relationship). Genetic panel (KCNQ1, KCNH2, KCNJ2, CACNA1C, CACNB2). EP study: short atrial/ventricular refractory periods, VF inducibility. Family screening mandatory.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ICD: mainstay for symptomatic
patients — careful programming mandatory
due to tall, peaked T-waves causing T-wave
oversensing. Quinidine or hydroquinidine for
ICD-ineligible patients (prolongs QT,
reduces VF inducibility). Family screening
with 12-lead ECG. Activity restriction
pending ICD placement.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Disopyramide for SQTS2
(KCNQ1-GOF). Genetic phenotype-specific
ion channel pharmacology under
investigation. S-ICD with careful QRS/T-
wave sensing optimization.

name: Noonan Syndrome (Cardiac)
description: RASopathy (PTPN11 in ~50%). Cardinal cardiac features: pulmonary stenosis (50-60%), HCM (20-30%), ASD. HCM in Noonan is often refractory and may progress rapidly in infancy.

frequency.sources: Romano et al., Eur J Med Genet 2010; Noonan ~1/1,000– 2,500 births; PTPN11 ~50%

diagnosis: Clinical: short stature, typical facies, cryptorchidism. Genetic panel (RASopathy genes). Echocardiography. ECG (left axis deviation). Surveillance echo for HCM progression.

treatment.standardOfCare: PS: balloon valvuloplasty (dysplastic valves have lower success rates than typical PS — may require surgical valvotomy). HCM: beta blockers, CCBs. Surgical myectomy for refractory LVOTO. ICD for high-risk HCM.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Trametinib (MEK inhibitor, Novartis) — FDA Breakthrough Designation
for HRAS/RAS pathway-mutant Noonan
HCM; active trials showing HCM regression.
Broader RASopathy-targeted therapies
(SHP2 inhibitors) for other Noonan variants.
Mavacamten for Noonan HCM with LVOTO
(off-label, emerging evidence).

name: Williams Syndrome / SVAS
description: Contiguous gene deletion syndrome (7q11.23; elastin gene ELN). SVAS present in ~75% and is the leading cause of morbidity. Sudden death risk during cardiac procedures due to bilateral coronary ostial involvement.

frequency.sources: Morris et al., Pediatrics 2010; Williams syndrome ~1/7,500 live births; ELN deletion 7q11.23

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis + FISH or chromosomal microarray for 7q11.23 deletion. Echo (SVAS gradient, coronary origins, branch PA stenosis). CT angiography for complex anatomy.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical SVAS repair (patch
aortoplasty — Doty or McGoon techniques)
for significant gradients. Peripheral PA
stenosis: transcatheter balloon dilation ±
stenting. Mandatory pre-anesthesia cardiac
evaluation due to SCD risk from coronary
ostial involvement or bilateral PA stenosis.
Lifelong cardiac surveillance.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Elastin augmentation strategies
targeting ELN haploinsufficiency.
Transcatheter SVAS approaches for discrete
membranous lesions. Improved coronary
ostial protection techniques perioperatively.

name: Alagille Syndrome (Cardiac)
description: Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder
diagnosis: Genetic testing (JAG1 or NOTCH2 sequencing). Clinical: cholestasis, butterfly vertebrae, posterior embryotoxon, triangular facies. Echo: RV pressure estimation. Cardiac MRI: quantitative bilateral PA blood flow, RV size and function. Cardiac catheterization + bilateral pulmonary angiography: gold standard for PA anatomy and pressures. Liver biopsy: bile duct paucity.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Transcatheter balloon pulmonary
arterioplasty and stenting: mainstay of catheterization management; serial
procedures throughout childhood targeting
sub-systemic RV pressure. Cutting balloon
and stent approaches for fibrotic lesions.
Liver transplantation for biliary cirrhosis
(~20–30%). Annual cardiac MRI and
Doppler echo for RV pressure tracking.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Odevixibat (Bylvay, Albireo, FDA
2021) for cholestasis in Alagille syndrome —
reduces pruritus and may slow liver disease
progression. JAG1/Notch pathway
modulation to promote PA growth
(preclinical). Drug-eluting balloons for
resistant PA stenosis.

name: CHARGE Syndrome
description: Autosomal dominant multisystem developmental disorder caused by CHD7 mutations (~90% of cases). Acronym: Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia choanae, Retardation of growth, Genital abnormalities, Ear anomalies with hearing loss. Cardiovascular malformations in ~75-80%; predominantly conotruncal: TOF (~20%), IAA, AVSD, VSD, PA- VSD, and complex heterotaxy. One of the most common causes of combined deaf-blindness in children.

frequency.sources: Zentner et al., Clin Genet 2010; CHARGE ~1/8,500– 12,000 births; CHD7 de novo mutation in ~60–70% FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis (Blake or Verloes criteria). CHD7 gene sequencing: positive in ~90%. Echo: complete cardiac anatomy. CT angiography for complex arch anatomy. Brain MRI: hypoplastic/absent semicircular canals (pathognomonic for CHARGE -- present in >90%). Choanal atresia: CT of nasal passages. Ophthalmology, audiology, endocrine evaluation.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Cardiac repair: standard surgical
management per specific defect. Sequential
choanal atresia + cardiac surgery
prioritization — choanal atresia repair first if
causing neonatal respiratory distress.
Anesthetic precautions: difficult airway,
absent balance system, sensorineural
hearing loss. Cochlear implantation for
profound deafness. GH replacement for GH
deficiency. Multidisciplinary management.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:CHD7-pathway targeted
therapies in preclinical development.
Improved sensorineural hearing
rehabilitation. Vestibular rehabilitation for
absent semicircular canals.

name: Congenital Heart Block
description: Disruption of AV conduction present from birth. Complete form occurs in ~1-2% of pregnancies with maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. Fetal complete heart block carries ~20-30% mortality without intervention.

frequency.sources: Congenital heart block ~1/20,000 births; anti-Ro/SSA antibody in neonatal autoimmune form

diagnosis: Fetal heart rate monitoring. Fetal echocardiography. Postnatal: ECG. Maternal autoantibody testing.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Fetal: maternal dexamethasone or
IVIG (limited efficacy for anti-Ro/SSA
antibody-mediated block). Postnatal:
permanent pacemaker implantation for
symptomatic complete heart block or resting
rate <55 bpm.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Hydroxychloroquine for anti-
Ro/SSA antibody-positive mothers in
subsequent pregnancies to prevent
recurrence (PATCH trial data). In utero
pacing — experimental. Beta-
sympathomimetics (isoproterenol) as
temporizing bridge in neonatal period.

name: Junctional Ectopic Tachycardia (JET)
description: Abnormal rhythm from the AV node. Postoperative JET occurs in ~1-5 per 1,000 pediatric cardiac surgeries. Congenital JET causes tachycardia- induced cardiomyopathy if rates remain persistently elevated.

frequency.us: ~1–10 new congenital JET US cases/yr; post-op JET ~500–2,500 US cases/yr
frequency.sources: Congenital JET very rare; postoperative JET ~1–5/1,000 pediatric cardiac surgeries

diagnosis: ECG (narrow complex tachycardia with AV dissociation). Holter for congenital JET.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Postoperative JET: amiodarone IV,
induced hypothermia (cooling to 34–35°C),
pacing above JET rate (overdrive atrial
pacing). Dexmedetomidine sedation.
Congenital JET: catheter ablation (80–90%
success using cryoablation near His to
reduce heart block risk).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Ivabradine (If channel blocker) for
postoperative JET — emerging case series
showing effective heart rate reduction
without negative inotropy; particularly useful
in low-output states. Cryoablation preferred
over RF near His bundle for congenital JET.

name: Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)
description: Rapid ventricular rhythm (>=3 beats, >120 bpm). May be idiopathic (benign RVOT-VT) or associated with structural disease, cardiomyopathy, or post- surgical scar.

frequency.us: ~2,000–5,000 new US pediatric VT cases/yr (clinically significant)
frequency.sources: Khairy et al., Circulation 2008; scar-related VT most prevalent in repaired TOF; ~0.2%/yr SCA risk

diagnosis: ECG. Holter/event monitor. Echocardiography. Cardiac MRI (scar assessment). EP study for catheter ablation planning.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ICD for high-risk structural VT or VF
survivors. Catheter ablation for idiopathic VT
(80–90% success — RVOT, fascicular,
papillary muscle). Antiarrhythmics
(amiodarone, mexiletine for scar-related VT).
Treat underlying structural cause.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Stereotactic body radiotherapy
(SBRT/cardiac radiosurgery) for refractory
scar-related VT not amenable to catheter
ablation — emerging as salvage therapy.
Pulsed-field ablation (PFA) under
investigation for VT substrate modification.

name: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
description: Most common significant pediatric arrhythmia. Rapid rhythm above ventricles -- most commonly AVRT (accessory pathway) or AVNRT. WPW syndrome carries risk of pre-excited AF and sudden death.

frequency.sources: AHA pediatric SVT guideline 2016; SVT ~1/250–1,000 children; WPW ~1– 3/1,000

diagnosis: ECG during episode. Adenosine for diagnosis and acute termination. Holter/event monitor. Delta wave on resting ECG identifies WPW.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Acute: vagal maneuvers, adenosine
IV. Long-term: catheter ablation (90–95%
cure rate for >15–20 kg). Definitive
treatment for high-risk WPW (shortest pre-
excited RR <250 ms) regardless of
symptoms. Beta blockers or flecainide for
suppression if ablation deferred.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Zero-fluoroscopy
electroanatomical mapping (CARTO,
EnSite) standard in pediatric centers —
reducing radiation exposure. Cryoablation
for para-Hisian and midseptal pathways —
lower heart block risk than RF.

name: Ectopic Atrial Tachycardia (EAT)
description: Sustained/incessant tachycardia from abnormal atrial focus. Incessant nature causes tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy in 25-50% of untreated cases.

frequency.us: ~7,300–10,950 US pediatric cases (10–15% of pediatric SVT)
frequency.sources: EAT ~10– 15% of pediatric SVT; automatic ectopic focus; LV dysfunction reverses with rate control

diagnosis: ECG (P-wave morphology differs from sinus; incessant pattern). Holter. Echo for LV function assessment.

treatment.standardOfCare: Antiarrhythmic agents (60–70% rate control): beta blockers, flecainide, sotalol, amiodarone. Catheter ablation preferred when accessible (80–90% success with high-density mapping). Beta blockers for suppression.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Ivabradine for rate control in medically refractory EAT — off-label but
effective without negative inotropy. High-
density electroanatomical mapping (Ripple
mapping, omnipolar technology) improving
ablation success for focal AT.

name: Atrial Flutter / Fibrillation
description: Flutter: organized rapid atrial rhythm (250-350 bpm). AFib: chaotic atrial activity. In children, often CHD-related; flutter common in Fontan patients (15-20% by adulthood).

frequency.us: ~1,800–3,600 new neonatal atrial flutter cases/yr; ~50,000–100,000 Fontan-IART US total
frequency.global: ~70,000– 140,000 new global neonatal atrial flutter cases/yr
frequency.sources: Neonatal atrial flutter ~1/10,000–20,000 births; intraatrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) in ~30–50% of Fontan patients by 10 yrs

diagnosis: ECG. Holter. Transesophageal echo for thrombus before cardioversion. EP study for ablation.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Acute: electrical cardioversion or
chemical cardioversion (ibutilide,
amiodarone). Catheter ablation: typical
flutter >90% cure; CHD-related intra-atrial
reentrant tachycardia (IART) 50–70%. Rate
control: beta blockers, digoxin.
Anticoagulation. Antiarrhythmics (sotalol,
amiodarone).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Pulsed-field ablation (PFA —
Farawave, Medtronic, FDA 2024) — non-
thermal ablation for AFib; entering CHD
population trials; may reduce risk of
collateral injury to esophagus/phrenic nerve.
High-density substrate mapping for complex
CHD-IART.

name: Sick Sinus Syndrome (SSS)
description: Sinus node dysfunction causing pathological bradycardia, chronotropic incompetence, sinus pauses, and tachy-brady syndrome. Two forms: (1) Congenital SSS -- associated with heterotaxy, L-TGA; (2) Post-operative SSS (more common) -- most common after Mustard/Senning, Fontan, ASD repair, and Maze procedures. Most common indication for permanent pacemaker implantation in the pediatric cardiac population. Tachy-brady syndrome is particularly dangerous: bradycardia causes syncope while tachyarrhythmia causes hemodynamic compromise and thromboembolism.

frequency.us: ~3,000–8,000 post- Mustard/Senning SSS cases; ~5,000– 15,000 post-Fontan SSS US total
frequency.sources: Post-op SSS after Mustard/Senning in ~20–40% by 20 yrs; post-Fontan SSS ~30–40% FREQUENCY

diagnosis: ECG: sinus bradycardia below age-appropriate lower limit, sinus pauses >3 seconds, prolonged post-tachycardia pause. Holter monitoring (24-72 hours or longer-term ILR): documents bradycardia- tachycardia alternation.
