Exercise stress test: chronotropic incompetence (failure to achieve >80% of maximum predicted heart rate). EP study: sinus node recovery time (SNRT).

treatment.standardOfCare: Permanent pacemaker (DDD/DDDR rate-responsive) for symptomatic SSS. Epicardial leads for small children or complex Fontan/Glenn anatomy. TREATMENT

name: Cardiac Rhabdomyoma
description: Most common primary cardiac tumor in children. Benign hamartoma of cardiac muscle; strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) in 50-80%. Most regress spontaneously; large or multiple tumors cause obstruction, arrhythmia, or heart failure.

frequency.us: ~360–720 new TSC-related rhabdomyoma cases/yr; ~730– 1,460 US total
frequency.sources: Cardiac rhabdomyoma ~1/100,000; ~50% of TSC patients; majority regress spontaneously

diagnosis: Fetal/neonatal echo (multiple echogenic masses). MRI for complex tumors. Genetic testing for TSC1/TSC2 mutations. EEG/MRI brain for TSC neurological involvement.

treatment.standardOfCare: Observation — majority regress spontaneously in infancy. Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor, FDA-approved for TSC) for TSC-associated rhabdomyomas causing hemodynamic compromise or arrhythmia. Surgical resection only for life-threatening obstruction not responding to medical therapy.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Sirolimus as alternative mTOR inhibitor. Prenatal diagnosis with in utero everolimus treatment under compassionate use protocols for hydrops/critical obstruction. Genetic testing for TSC1/TSC2 to guide therapy and family counseling.

name: Cardiac Fibroma
description: Second most common primary cardiac tumor in children. Benign fibrous tumor, non-regressing. Associated with Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1) in ~3%. Causes ventricular obstruction, arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death.

frequency.sources: Cardiac fibroma <1/100,000; significant SCD risk from VT/VF in large interventricular lesions

diagnosis: Echocardiography (large, echogenic, non-contractile intramyocardial mass). Cardiac MRI (central fibrous 'dark' appearance on LGE -- pathognomonic). Genetic testing for Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical resection (partial or complete)
for large symptomatic tumors. ICD for
VT/SCD prevention. Catheter ablation for
arrhythmia arising from fibroma. Cardiac
transplantation for unresectable tumors
causing severe HF.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Hedgehog pathway inhibition
(vismodegib for PTCH1-associated fibromas
in Gorlin syndrome) under investigation.
MRI-guided cardiac mapping to define
arrhythmia substrate within fibroma.
Cryoablation as adjunct to partial resection.

name: Cardiac Myxoma (Pediatric)
description: Most common benign cardiac tumor overall but rare in children. Gelatinous polypoid mass usually arising from the interatrial septum. Causes obstruction, systemic embolism, and constitutional symptoms. Carney complex (PRKAR1A mutation) associated in ~10% of pediatric myxomas.

frequency.us: ~10–18 new US pediatric cases/yr (<5% of all cardiac myxomas)
frequency.sources: Cardiac myxoma most common benign cardiac tumor in adults; <5% in children under 15

diagnosis: Echocardiography (pedunculated mobile mass attached to fossa ovalis). Cardiac MRI. Genetic testing for PRKAR1A (Carney complex). Ophthalmology exam if Carney complex suspected.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical excision with wide margins
(and base of stalk) — curative. Carney
complex: echo surveillance every 12 months
lifelong due to high recurrence risk (~20%).
Anticoagulation for embolic events.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:PRKAR1A genetic screening for
Carney complex family members. Minimally
invasive/thoracoscopic excision for recurrent
myxoma in selected anatomy. Improved
imaging (cardiac MRI) for tumor
characterization and pre-operative planning.

name: Intrapericardial Teratoma
description: Germ cell tumor arising within the pericardial space, attached to the root of the aorta or pulmonary artery. Not intracardiac -- compresses the heart from the outside. The most common pericardial/cardiac tumor of the fetus and neonate and the most common cause of large fetal pericardial effusion. The effusion causes cardiac tamponade, fetal hydrops, and -- if untreated -- fetal or neonatal death. Histologically benign in the vast majority; postnatal surgical excision is curative.

frequency.sources: Most common cardiac/pericardial tumor presenting in utero or neonatal period

diagnosis: Fetal echo: large pericardial effusion with echogenic heterogeneous mass at the base of the great vessels -- virtually pathognomonic. Fetal MRI: mass anatomy and relationship to great vessel roots. Postnatal echo and CT for surgical planning. AFP: elevated in fetal and neonatal serum (germ cell origin).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Fetal: pericardiocentesis for hydrops threatening fetal demise (temporizing). Delivery planning at center with immediate
postnatal surgical capability. Postnatal:
complete surgical excision — curative; CPB
often not required. ECMO for pre-operative
hemodynamic instability. Adjuvant
chemotherapy for malignant/immature
teratoma (BEP regimen).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:EXIT (ex utero intrapartum
treatment) procedure for large tumors
causing airway compromise at delivery.
Fetal MRI for precise tumor characterization
and surgical planning. Minimally invasive
resection for smaller, extrapericardially
accessible tumors.

name: Cardiac Rhabdomyosarcoma
description: Most common primary malignant cardiac tumor in children. Arises from cardiac striated muscle (most commonly ventricular myocardium or AV valves) and is locally invasive. Unlike benign pediatric cardiac tumors, rhabdomyosarcoma is aggressive with local invasion of cardiac structures and hematogenous metastasis. There is no spontaneous regression. Complete surgical resection is rarely achievable due to local invasion.

frequency.us: ~10–25 new US primary cardiac rhabdomyosarcoma cases/yr
frequency.sources: Primary cardiac rhabdomyosarcoma ~25% of primary malignant cardiac tumors; extremely rare FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Echo: large, irregular, invasive-appearing cardiac mass -- often infiltrates rather than displaces normal structures (unlike benign tumors). Cardiac MRI: tissue characterization, extent of invasion, pericardial involvement. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging. PET scan for systemic staging. Tissue biopsy: essential for diagnosis and histological subtype.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Multidisciplinary management (cardiac
surgery + pediatric oncology). Surgical
debulking to relieve obstruction and obtain
tissue; complete resection rarely possible.
Adjuvant chemotherapy: VAC regimen
(vincristine, actinomycin D,
cyclophosphamide) — standard
rhabdomyosarcoma protocol. Radiation
therapy for local control. Palliative intent
frequently the realistic goal.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) +
chemotherapy combinations in pediatric
rhabdomyosarcoma trials. CDK4/6 inhibitors
and MDM2 antagonists for specific genomic
subsets. CAR-T cell approaches targeting
RMS-associated antigens in early trials.

name: Kawasaki Disease
description: Acute self-limited vasculitis preferentially targeting the coronary arteries. Leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. Coronary artery aneurysms develop in 20- 25% of untreated children.

frequency.us: cases annually. US: ~72,000– 160,000 new US cases/yr (children under 5); ~4,500– 9,000 coronary aneurysm cases/yr
frequency.sources: McCrindle et al., AHA Circulation 2017; 9– 20/100,000 US children under 5; Japan ~300/100,000 (highest globally)

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis: fever >=5 days plus >=4 of 5 classic features (rash, conjunctival injection, mucous membrane changes, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Echo at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks for coronary assessment.

treatment.standardOfCare:
High-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) + aspirin
within first 10 days (reduces aneurysm risk
to <5%). Corticosteroids as adjunctive
therapy or for IVIG-resistant cases. Long-
term anticoagulation (warfarin + low-dose
aspirin) for giant aneurysms. Surveillance
catheterization for giant aneurysms with
stenosis.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Infliximab (TNF inhibitor) for
IVIG-resistant KD — comparable efficacy to
second IVIG dose with fewer infusion
reactions; now widely used at many centers.
Cyclosporine for refractory KD. Anakinra (IL-
1Ra) for severe refractory cases. Predictive
scoring tools (Kobayashi, Egami) to identify
IVIG resistance risk pre-treatment.

name: MIS-C (Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)
description: Post-infectious hyperinflammatory syndrome occurring 2-6 weeks after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Causes myocarditis, coronary artery dilation, ventricular dysfunction, and shock.

frequency.us: through 2023. US: ~3,500–5,000 new US cases during 2020–2023 peak; ~600– 1,000/yr from 2023 onward
frequency.global: ~50,000– 150,000 total global cases reported (CDC, WHO surveillance through 2024)
frequency.sources: Feldstein et al., NEJM 2020; CDC MIS-C surveillance; incidence markedly decreased with Omicron variant + vaccination

diagnosis: CDC case definition: fever + elevated inflammatory markers + multiorgan involvement + SARS- CoV-2 evidence. Echo (LV dysfunction, coronary artery Z-scores). Troponin, BNP. Inflammatory markers (CRP, ferritin, D-dimer).

treatment.standardOfCare: IVIG (2 g/kg) + aspirin. Corticosteroids for refractory or severe cases. Hemodynamic support: inotropes, ECMO for severe cardiogenic shock. Anticoagulation for coronary dilation (z-score ≥2.5) or significant LV dysfunction.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) for refractory MIS-C with macrophage activation syndrome features. Standardized cardiac MRI follow-up protocols to assess myocardial recovery. Long-term data on coronary outcomes and
myocardial fibrosis accumulating.

name: Infective Endocarditis (IE)
description: Infection of the endocardial surface of the heart, predominantly affecting cardiac valves. In children, predominantly affects those with underlying CHD (VSDs, AVSDs, TOF, prosthetic valves, indwelling lines). Organisms: Streptococcus viridans group (most common), Staphylococcus aureus (most aggressive).

frequency.us: ~215–360 new US pediatric cases/yr; ~10,000– 20,000 in high-risk CHD populations/yr
frequency.sources: Baltimore et al., Circulation 2015; IE ~0.3–0.5/100,000 children/yr in structurally normal hearts; 5–10/1,000 person-yrs in high- risk CHD

diagnosis: Duke Criteria (modified 2000). Echocardiography (TTE first, TEE for prosthetic valves). Blood cultures x3 before antibiotics.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Prolonged IV antibiotics (4–6 weeks;
organism-directed per blood culture
sensitivities). Empirical anti-staphylococcal
coverage until cultures available
(vancomycin or daptomycin). Early surgical
consultation for: HF from valvular
destruction, persistent bacteremia, large
vegetations (>10 mm), perivalvular abscess.
Dental prophylaxis for high-risk CHD.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Bacteriophage therapy for
prosthetic valve IE caused by resistant
organisms (compassionate use, case
series). Biofilm-targeted antibiotics
(daptomycin + rifampin combinations).
Updated AHA/ACC 2023 IE guidelines:
dental prophylaxis indications refined;
broader cardiac device IE management.

name: Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD)
description: Autoimmune valvular damage triggered by repeated Group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Leading cause of acquired heart disease in children globally. Mitral valve affected in >80% of cases.

frequency.sources: WHO GHO; RHD ~500– 1,000/100,000 school-age in endemic regions; essentially rare in high-income countries

diagnosis: Clinical history of rheumatic fever. Echocardiography per World Heart Federation criteria. Throat culture or rapid strep test for acute GAS pharyngitis.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Secondary prophylaxis: monthly benzathine penicillin G for 10 years or until age 25 (whichever longer) to prevent recurrent GAS pharyngitis and rheumatic
fever. Surgical valve repair or replacement
for advanced valvular disease.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Group A streptococcal (M-protein
based) vaccine — multiple candidates in
Phase 2/3 trials; would be transformative for
RHD prevention globally. Transcatheter
mitral valve repair (MitraClip) for severe
RHD-MR in resource-limited settings where
surgery unavailable.

name: Acute Pericarditis
description: Inflammation of the pericardium causing chest pain, pericardial friction rub, and characteristic ECG changes (diffuse ST elevation, PR depression). Most commonly viral. Can progress to pericardial effusion and tamponade.

frequency.sources: Imazio et al., Circulation 2007; ~1–2/100,000 children/yr; recurrent pericarditis in 15–30%

diagnosis: ECG (diffuse saddle- shaped ST elevation, PR depression). Echo (pericardial effusion, rule out tamponade). Cardiac MRI (pericardial inflammation on LGE). Troponin (elevated if myopericarditis). CRP, ESR.

treatment.standardOfCare:
NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600 mg TID or
aspirin) — first-line for 2–4 weeks.
Colchicine add-on (reduces recurrence by
~50%; COPE and ICAP trials).
Corticosteroids for NSAID-refractory or
autoimmune pericarditis. Exercise restriction
for 3 months. Treat underlying cause.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Rilonacept (Arcalyst, Regeneron,
FDA 2021) — IL-1α/β inhibitor; approved for
recurrent pericarditis refractory to colchicine
(RHAPSODY trial). Anakinra (IL-1 receptor
antagonist) for colchicine-refractory and IL-
1-driven recurrent pericarditis; particularly in
pediatrics. Pericardiectomy for constrictive
pericarditis (see entry 84).

name: Constrictive Pericarditis
description: Progressive fibrosis and calcification of the pericardium that encases and constricts the heart, impairing diastolic ventricular filling. In children, most commonly follows viral pericarditis, post-cardiac surgery (post- pericardiotomy syndrome), or TB pericarditis in endemic regions. Critically important distinction from restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM, #38): constrictive pericarditis is surgically curable; RCM is not. The two conditions produce identical clinical presentations, requiring catheterization and MRI for differentiation.

frequency.sources: 5–10% of children with acute pericarditis develop some degree of constriction

diagnosis: Echo: septal bounce (pathognomonic -- interventricular septal shift with respiration), biatrial enlargement, normal LVEF, annulus reversus (medial mitral annular e' > lateral e' on tissue Doppler). CT: pericardial thickening (>4mm) and calcification. Cardiac MRI: pericardial thickness, LGE, ventricular interdependence. Cardiac catheterization (gold standard): equalization of diastolic pressures; dip- and-plateau ('square root sign'); discordant ventricular pressure changes with respiration (key differentiator from RCM).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surgical pericardiectomy (radical pericardial decortication of both ventricles, visceral and parietal) — definitive and curative. Complete pericardiectomy essential for lasting hemodynamic benefit. Anti-inflammatory therapy (NSAIDs + colchicine) for early/effusive-constrictive
disease — ~20–30% resolve without
surgery. Antituberculous therapy mandated
for TB pericarditis. Diuretics for venous
congestion while awaiting surgery.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Video-assisted thoracoscopic
pericardiectomy (VATS) for selected cases
— reduced morbidity vs. median
sternotomy/thoracotomy. Cardiac MRI with
LGE to identify pericardial
fibrosis/inflammation and predict surgical
benefit vs. spontaneous resolution.

name: Aortic Valve Regurgitation (Acquired/Post- Interventional)
description: Progressive regurgitation of the aortic valve resulting from congenital valve disease, prior balloon valvuloplasty, prior surgical valvotomy, infective endocarditis, rheumatic disease, or Ross procedure failure. A leading reason for re- intervention in patients with prior LVOT disease.

frequency.us: ~5,000–12,000 US prevalent pediatric cases (post-intervention aortic regurgitation)
frequency.sources: Post- balloon valvuloplasty AR in 20–40% of neonatal/infant aortic interventions FREQUENCY

diagnosis: Echo: AR jet width, vena contracta, holodiastolic reversal in descending aorta. Cardiac MRI: gold standard for AR quantification (regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction) and LV end- systolic volume index (LVESVi -- intervention threshold >=25 mL/m2). Serial surveillance echo every 6-12 months.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Surveillance to LV thresholds (LVESVi
≥25 mL/m², LVEF <50%, or symptoms).
Ross or Ozaki procedure preferred in
children and young adults. Mechanical valve
replacement when repair criteria not met.
TAVR valve-in-valve for failed bioprosthetic
aortic valves in adolescents/adults.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Ozaki procedure (aortic valve
neocuspidization with autologous
pericardium) gaining broad adoption as
Ross alternative — avoids pulmonary
autograft reoperation. BASILICA technique
(pre-TAVR leaflet laceration) to prevent
coronary occlusion during valve-in-valve
TAVR. Transcatheter aortic valve repair
approaches in development.

name: Post-Cardiotomy Syndrome / Low Cardiac Output (LCOS)
description: Systemic inflammatory and hemodynamic response following cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), manifesting as clinically significant low cardiac output (CI <2.0 L/min/m2). Caused by myocardial ischemia- reperfusion injury, complement activation from bypass circuit contact, capillary leak, and post-operative systemic vasoconstriction. The leading perioperative cause of CICU morbidity and mortality in pediatric cardiac surgery.

frequency.us: ~8,750–12,250 new US pediatric post-cardiotomy LCOS cases/yr
frequency.sources: Hoffman et al., Semin Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2003; LCOS in 25– 35% of post- cardiotomy patients in first 24 hrs

diagnosis: NIRS (near-infrared spectroscopy) -- continuous regional O2 saturation; falling cerebral NIRS is an early LCOS indicator. Arterial line (continuous BP, blood gas access). Central venous line (filling pressures). Mixed venous SvO2 or SvcO2 (target >65-70%). Cardiac index measurement. Lactate trends (rising lactate = early LCOS indicator). Echo (LVEF, RV function, tamponade, residual lesions).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Optimize preload (CVP target 8–12
mmHg). Milrinone (first-line — prophylactic
milrinone post-neonatal surgery reduces
LCOS incidence by 64%, PRIMACORP
trial). Epinephrine, dopamine for refractory
cases. Vasopressin for vasodilatory shock.
ECMO rescue for refractory LCOS (VA
configuration; survival 40–60%).
Neuromuscular blockade and sedation to
reduce O2 demand.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Levosimendan (calcium
sensitizer/K-ATP channel opener) as
alternative/adjunct to milrinone — emerging
evidence for lower risk of tachyarrhythmia
vs. catecholamines. Terlipressin (V1a
agonist) for vasodilatory shock post-CPB in
pediatric centers.

name: Pulmonary Hypertensive Crisis (Post-Operative)
description: Sudden, severe elevation in pulmonary vascular resistance causing acute RV failure and hemodynamic collapse. A distinct life-threatening event from chronic PAH. Occurs in the early post- operative period in patients with CHD and pre-existing pulmonary hypertension. Triggered by hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, suctioning, pain, or stimulation.

frequency.us: arteriosus, TAPVR with delayed repair, and patients with Down syndrome. US: ~500–1,250 new US pediatric post-op PHC cases/yr
frequency.sources: Occurs in ~5–10% of patients with pre-existing elevated PVR undergoing CHD surgery

diagnosis: Clinical: sudden acute desaturation, hypotension, bradycardia, loss of pulse pressure. PA line: acute rise in PA pressures approaching or exceeding systemic systolic. NIRS: acute drop in cerebral saturation. Echo: acute RV dilation, septal shift, reduced PA flow. ABG: hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis.

treatment.standardOfCare: Hyperventilation (pCO2 target 30–35 mmHg). 100% FiO2. Inhaled nitric oxide (20–40 ppm) — first-line pharmacological therapy. IV sildenafil for iNO transition/weaning. Alkalinization (sodium bicarbonate). Deep sedation + neuromuscular blockade. Minimize stimulation. Prostacyclin (inhaled or IV) for iNO-refractory cases. ECMO for refractory PH crisis with hemodynamic collapse.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Inhaled treprostinil as alternative/adjunct to iNO for post-operative PH. Transition protocols from iNO to oral/inhaled PAH therapy (sildenafil, bosentan) to facilitate safe weaning. Riociguat (sGC stimulator) for post-operative
PH in adults.

name: Cardiac Tamponade
description: Pericardial fluid accumulation causing external cardiac compression, impaired ventricular filling, and obstructive cardiogenic shock. In the CICU, most commonly post-operative. Also occurs in myopericarditis, pericarditis, malignancy, and post-cardiac procedure.

frequency.us: ~500–2,500 new US pediatric cardiac tamponade cases/yr (post- cardiac surgery)
frequency.sources: Post- cardiac surgery tamponade in ~1– 5% of pediatric cardiac surgeries

diagnosis: Beck's triad: hypotension + elevated JVP + muffled heart sounds (late and insensitive). Echo: pericardial effusion + RA/RV collapse in diastole + plethoric IVC + respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow >25% (pathognomonic). Pulsus paradoxus: BP drop >10 mmHg on inspiration. CXR: enlarged cardiac silhouette.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Emergency ultrasound-guided
pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid or apical
approach). Surgical drainage for: post-
operative hemorrhagic tamponade, posterior
effusions not accessible by needle, clotted
effusions. IV fluid bolus as temporizing
bridge. Avoid positive pressure ventilation
(reduces venous return, worsens
tamponade).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Point-of-care ultrasound
(POCUS) for real-time guidance becoming
standard. Percutaneous balloon
pericardiotomy for recurrent malignant
effusions. Pericardioscopy-guided
pericardiocentesis for complex or loculated
effusions.

name: Chylothorax
description: Accumulation of chyle (lymphatic fluid rich in triglycerides and lymphocytes) in the pleural space due to injury to or obstruction of the thoracic duct during cardiac surgery. Most common after Glenn and Fontan procedures, arch surgery, BT shunt, and mediastinal dissection.

frequency.sources: Chylothorax in 1–3% of pediatric cardiac surgeries overall; higher rates after Glenn/Fontan (5–8%)

diagnosis: Pleural fluid analysis: triglycerides >110 mg/dL (diagnostic). Lymphocyte predominance >80%. Daily chest tube output tracking. Chest radiograph/ultrasound. MR lymphangiography for thoracic duct anatomy and leak localization.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Conservative: MCT diet, NPO with TPN for high-output chylothorax. Octreotide (somatostatin analog) IV or SQ. Chest tube drainage. Thoracic duct embolization (Itkin technique via cisterna chyli, 80–90% closure) — increasingly preferred over
surgery. Surgical thoracic duct ligation for
embolization failures. Pleurodesis for
recalcitrant cases.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) for
chylous effusions — particularly Fontan-
related chylothorax and
lymphangioleiomyomatosis-related; active
clinical use at many centers. Intranodal
lymphangiography + embolization refining
technique.

name: Diaphragm Paralysis (Phrenic Nerve Injury)
description: Injury to the phrenic nerve during cardiac surgery causing unilateral or bilateral diaphragmatic paralysis. Left phrenic nerve most commonly affected due to its proximity to the aortic arch, left PA, and ductus arteriosus dissection. Results in paradoxical diaphragmatic movement, reduced lung volumes, atelectasis, and prolonged ventilator dependence.

frequency.us: ~500–2,500 new US pediatric phrenic nerve injury cases/yr
frequency.sources: Phrenic nerve injury in 1–5% of pediatric cardiac surgeries; higher rates in neonatal/infant operations

diagnosis: Difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation without explanation. Ultrasound: bedside assessment of diaphragm motion -- gold standard; paradoxical motion is diagnostic. CXR: elevated hemidiaphragm. Fluoroscopy: sniff test.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Trial of non-invasive ventilation
(BiPAP/CPAP) post-extubation (positioning
affected side up, chest physiotherapy).
Surgical diaphragm plication: definitive
treatment for failed extubation;
thoracoscopic approach preferred; after 4–6
weeks conservative trial (or immediately for
bilateral paralysis).
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Robot-assisted thoracoscopic
diaphragm plication — reduced morbidity,
comparable outcomes. Diaphragm pacing
(phrenic nerve stimulation) for bilateral
paralysis in selected cases. Ultrasound-
guided assessment of diaphragm excursion
to monitor recovery before committing to
plication.

name: Protein-Losing Enteropathy (PLE) in Fontan
description: Life-limiting complication of Fontan circulation in which protein (predominantly albumin) leaks from the gut into the intestinal lumen due to chronically elevated systemic venous pressure and lymphatic hypertension. Results in hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, ascites, pleural effusions, and immune deficiency. Five-year survival after PLE diagnosis is ~50%.

frequency.sources: Affects 3– 15% of Fontan patients; onset typically 2–10 years after Fontan completion

diagnosis: Clinical: peripheral edema, ascites, pleural effusions, facial edema, diarrhea. Serum albumin <3.5 g/dL. Alpha-1- antitrypsin clearance. 99mTc-labeled albumin nuclear scan -- localizes gut protein loss. Cardiac catheterization for hemodynamic assessment. MR lymphangiography.

treatment.standardOfCare:
High-protein, fat-restricted (MCT fat)
diet. Sodium and fluid restriction.
Spironolactone + diuretics. Subcutaneous
UFH (100 units/kg/day). Sildenafil.
Budesonide (oral). Albumin infusions for
acute decompensation. Catheter-created
Fontan fenestration to decompress systemic
venous pressure. Heart transplantation for medically refractory PLE.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Thoracic lymphatic embolization
(Fontan-specific lymphatic intervention —
Itkin/CHOP protocol): emerging as major
catheter-based intervention for PLE and
plastic bronchitis; directly decompresses
lymphatic hypertension.

name: Plastic Bronchitis in Fontan
description: Rare but potentially fatal complication of Fontan circulation in which bronchial casts composed of lymphatic fluid and inflammatory cells fill and obstruct the bronchial tree. Patients expectorate rigid, branching casts that replicate the bronchial anatomy. Pathophysiology: lymphatic hypertension from elevated Fontan venous pressure causes lymphatic fluid to leak into the airways.

frequency.us: ~100–400 US total Fontan plastic bronchitis cases
frequency.sources: Prevalence ~1–4% in Fontan population; mortality per acute episode ~10–15%

diagnosis: Clinical: acute respiratory distress, hypoxemia, expectorated or bronchoscopically retrieved branching casts (diagnostic). CT chest: branching hyperdense opacities filling the bronchi. Bronchoscopy: direct visualization and retrieval of bronchial casts. Echo/catheterization: Fontan hemodynamic assessment. MR lymphangiography.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Acute: bronchoscopy for cast removal.
Inhaled tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
— standard of care at experienced centers;
dissolves fibrin casts and reduces
recurrence. Chest physiotherapy + airway
clearance. Inhaled heparin (reduces cast
formation). Optimize Fontan hemodynamics:
sildenafil, bosentan. Heart transplantation
for medically refractory plastic bronchitis.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Thoracic lymphatic embolization
— same as PLE; increasingly effective for
plastic bronchitis via lymphatic
decompression. Inhaled dornase alfa as
mucolytic adjunct. Combined heart-liver
transplantation for cases with advanced
FALD.

name: Fontan-Associated Liver Disease (FALD)
description: Progressive hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma resulting from chronic elevation of systemic venous pressure transmitted to the hepatic venous system in Fontan physiology. Nearly universal in long-term Fontan survivors. A leading cause of late morbidity and mortality in Fontan patients.

frequency.sources: Hepatic fibrosis present in virtually all Fontan patients within 10 years; cirrhosis ~50% by 20 years

diagnosis: Liver function tests (often normal until late disease; elevated GGT may be early marker). Serum elastography (FibroScan) -- non-invasive fibrosis staging. MRI liver: fibrosis, nodularity, HCC surveillance. AFP (HCC marker) -- annual. Liver biopsy: gold standard (used selectively). Hepatology co- management from 5-10 years post-Fontan.

treatment.standardOfCare: No disease-modifying therapy proven to prevent or reverse FALD. Optimize Fontan hemodynamics to reduce hepatic venous pressure. Avoid hepatotoxic medications. HCC surveillance: 6-monthly AFP + annual liver MRI from 10 years post- Fontan. HCC treatment: resection or ablation if isolated. Combined heart-liver transplantation for advanced hepatic fibrosis + Fontan failure.
treatment.emerging: Emerging:Non-invasive liver fibrosis staging (FibroScan/transient elastography, MR elastography) to monitor progression without biopsy. Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone, nintedanib) under investigation for FALD. FIB-4 score and hepatic venous pressure gradient as surveillance markers.

name: Fontan Failure
description: Progressive deterioration of Fontan physiology characterized by falling cardiac output, rising Fontan pressures, and multiorgan dysfunction. Clinical syndrome: low cardiac output, ascites, edema, pleural effusions, PLE, plastic bronchitis, FALD, and arrhythmias. The final common pathway for all Fontan patients if they survive long enough.

frequency.us: ~7,200–14,400 US Fontan patients at risk (40–50% by age 40)
frequency.sources: Estimated 40–50% of Fontan patients develop significant failure by age 40

diagnosis: Echocardiography (ventricular function, AV valve regurgitation, Fontan pathway obstruction). Cardiac catheterization (Fontan pressure, PVR, cardiac output -- essential before transplantation listing). MRI (ventricular volumes and function). Liver assessment (FALD staging). PLE evaluation. Renal function. Functional assessment: 6-minute walk test, VO2 max.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Medical optimization: diuretics,
afterload reduction, pulmonary vasodilators
(sildenafil, bosentan). Rhythm management:
antiarrhythmics, catheter ablation for IART.
Catheter interventions: Fontan fenestration,
Fontan pathway stenting for conduit
obstruction, APC coil embolization. Fontan
conversion surgery for failing atriopulmonary
connections. Heart transplantation — the
only definitive therapy. Combined heart-liver
transplantation for advanced FALD.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Mechanical cavopulmonary
assist (percutaneous TCPC pump — Fontan
mechanical assist device trials). Thoracic
lymphatic embolization for PLE/plastic
bronchitis. Fenestration optimization with
adjustable devices.

name: Acute Cellular Rejection (Post-Cardiac Transplant)
description: T-cell-mediated immune response against the transplanted heart. The primary cause of morbidity and death in the first year after cardiac transplantation. Graded by the ISHLT rejection grading system (0-3R based on endomyocardial biopsy histology).

frequency.us: ~400–800 new US pediatric transplant rejection episodes/yr
frequency.sources: Treated rejection episodes in 20–40% of pediatric recipients in first year post-transplant

diagnosis: Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB): gold standard for diagnosis and grading (ISHLT grade 1R = mild; 2R = moderate; 3R = severe). EMB protocol: biweekly for first 2 months, monthly until year 1, then annually. Echo: LV dysfunction, new wall motion abnormality. Biomarkers: troponin, BNP. Gene expression profiling (AlloMap).

treatment.standardOfCare: Grade 1R: optimize oral immunosuppression; close follow-up. Grade 2R or 3R: IV methylprednisolone pulse (10– 30 mg/kg/day × 3 days, max 1 g/day). Grade 3R refractory to steroids: rabbit ATG. AMR: plasmapheresis + IVIG + rituximab. Hemodynamic support: inotropes, ECMO as bridge to recovery. Maintenance immunosuppression optimization.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor) for refractory AMR — reduces plasma cell burden. C1-esterase inhibitor (Berinert) for complement-mediated AMR.
Belatacept (CTLA4-Ig) as calcineurin
inhibitor alternative. Non-invasive rejection
surveillance: donor-derived cell-free DNA
(dd-cfDNA) as liquid biopsy.

name: Primary Graft Dysfunction (PGD)
description: Severe cardiac dysfunction of the transplanted heart occurring within 24 hours of implantation. Results from ischemia-reperfusion injury, prolonged ischemic time, donor-recipient size mismatch, and pre-existing donor cardiac dysfunction. The leading cause of early post-transplant death, often requiring ECMO.

frequency.sources: PGD in 10– 20% of cardiac transplant recipients; severe PGD requiring ECMO in ~3–5%

diagnosis: Clinical presentation: failure to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass, or acute severe hemodynamic deterioration within first 24 hours. Echo: severe biventricular dysfunction (EF <40%). Right heart catheterization: low cardiac output, elevated filling pressures. Exclusion of: anastomotic complications, hyperacute rejection.

treatment.standardOfCare:
ECMO: primary rescue for severe PGD
(VA configuration). Inotropes: epinephrine,
milrinone, vasopressin. Inhaled nitric oxide
for RV failure component. ECMO weaning
when graft recovery sufficient (typically 48–
96 hours). VAD as bridge to re-
transplantation if no recovery. Prevention:
minimize ischemic time, optimize donor
management.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Ex vivo heart perfusion (EVHP —
Transmedics OCS Heart): extends ischemic
tolerance, allows real-time graft assessment,
enables use of marginal donor hearts.
Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) for
DCD (donation after circulatory death)
hearts — expanding donor pool.

name: Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy (CAV)
description: Accelerated, diffuse coronary artery disease affecting the transplanted heart, caused by chronic immune-mediated vascular injury. Unlike native coronary artery disease, CAV affects the entire coronary tree diffusely and concentrically. The leading cause of death in pediatric cardiac transplant recipients beyond the first year.

frequency.us: ~750–1,000 US pediatric CAV cases; ~3,000– 5,000 US total (all ages)
frequency.sources: CAV present in ~30% of pediatric recipients by 5 years and ~50% by 10 years on IVUS

diagnosis: Annual coronary assessment: cardiac catheterization with IVUS (gold standard -- detects CAV before angiographic changes). Coronary angiography (underestimates disease extent). Dobutamine stress echo (functional ischemia assessment). Surveillance: annually from year 1 post- transplant. Biomarkers: donor-specific antibodies (DSA) -- major risk factor for CAV.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Statin therapy from day 1 post- transplant (reduces CAV progression). Everolimus or sirolimus (mTOR inhibitors): most evidence for slowing CAV — switch from azathioprine in patients with early CAV.
Optimize immunosuppression. Treat DSA:
plasmapheresis + IVIG + rituximab. PCI for
focal lesions. Retransplantation for
advanced CAV.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Belatacept (CTLA4-Ig) as
calcineurin-sparing strategy to reduce
nephrotoxicity while maintaining
immunosuppression. OCT (optical
coherence tomography) for early intimal
thickness quantification and CAV staging.
dd-cfDNA as liquid biopsy for subclinical
rejection monitoring.

name: Post-Transplant Lymphoproliferative Disorder (PTLD)
description: EBV-driven lymphoid proliferation occurring in immunosuppressed cardiac transplant recipients, ranging from benign polyclonal hyperplasia to aggressive monoclonal lymphoma. Pediatric recipients at highest risk because most are EBV-naive at transplantation.

frequency.sources: PTLD incidence ~5–15% in pediatric cardiac transplant recipients; EBV- naive recipients highest risk FREQUENCY

diagnosis: EBV viral load monitoring: quantitative PCR for EBV DNA (surveillance every 1-3 months in first 2 years). Rising EBV viral load precedes PTLD development. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: lymphadenopathy, mass lesions. PET scan for staging. Tissue biopsy: definitive diagnosis and WHO classification.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Immunosuppression reduction (first-
line — induces remission in ~30–50% of
early polyclonal PTLD). Rituximab (anti-
CD20): first-line for CD20+ B-cell PTLD
(>90% of pediatric PTLD). CHOP-based
chemotherapy for refractory or aggressive
monoclonal PTLD. Ganciclovir/valganciclovir
prophylaxis in EBV-naive recipients.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:EBV-specific cytotoxic T-
lymphocyte (CTL) adoptive immunotherapy
— available at specialized centers; highly
effective for EBV+ PTLD. PD-1 checkpoint
inhibitors (pembrolizumab) for refractory
PTLD (caution: rejection risk — use with
augmented immunosuppression).

name: Branch Pulmonary Artery Stenosis
description: Narrowing of the left and/or right pulmonary artery branches and their segmental/subsegmental divisions. Occurs as a congenital lesion or, more commonly, post- operatively following repair of TOF, truncus arteriosus, TAPVR, PA-VSD, and after Glenn/Fontan procedures. Causes elevated RV pressure, RV hypertrophy and failure, and reduced pulmonary blood flow to affected lung segments.

frequency.us: arteriosus repairs, and essentially all patients with PA- VSD/MAPCAs. Williams syndrome causes severe diffuse peripheral PA stenosis in ~75- 90% of patients. US: ~5,000–15,000 US total (all degrees); ~1,000– 3,000 clinically significant
frequency.sources: Post- operative PA stenosis virtually universal after PA- related CHD repairs; clinically significant in ~5–20%

diagnosis: Echo with Doppler (RV pressure estimation via TR jet velocity). Cardiac MRI: gold standard for bilateral branch PA assessment and differential lung blood flow quantification. Cardiac catheterization + angiography: pressure gradient measurement (>20 mmHg generally warrants intervention). CT angiography for segmental/subsegmental anatomy. Radionuclide perfusion scan (V/Q) for differential lung flow.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Transcatheter balloon pulmonary
arterioplasty (initial treatment for discrete
stenoses). PA stenting with bare metal
stents (allows re-dilation as child grows —
preferred for most significant lesions).
Cutting balloon for fibrotic or elastic recoil
lesions. Surgical arterioplasty for bifurcation
stenoses not catheter-accessible.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Drug-eluting stents (sirolimus-
eluting) for PA stenosis — under
investigation to reduce restenosis. High-
pressure compliant balloons (ATLAS
balloon) for resistant lesions. Drug-eluting
balloons (paclitaxel-coated) for restenotic
lesions. Biodegradable vascular scaffolds in
early research.

name: RV-PA Conduit Failure
description: Stenosis and/or regurgitation of right

frequency.us: live with an RV-PA conduit. Melody Valve (Medtronic, FDA 2010) and SAPIEN XT/3 (Edwards, FDA 2016) have collectively performed >50,000 TPVR procedures
frequency.sources: Conduit failure requiring intervention in virtually all recipients over time; median conduit longevity ~10–15 yrs

diagnosis: Echo: Doppler-estimated conduit gradient, degree

treatment.standardOfCare:
TPVR: preferred for suitable conduit anatomy. Melody valve (conduits 14–28 mm). SAPIEN 3 (conduits/native RVOT 19–
29 mm). Harmony TPV (native RVOT, FDA
2021). Coronary compression test
mandatory before implantation. Surgical
conduit replacement when conduit too large,
calcified, or TPVR coronary compression
risk prohibitive.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Harmony TPV22 (next-
generation, broader sizing) for dilated native
RVOT. COMPASSION trials expanding
TPVR to non-circular/dilated native RVOT.
Tissue-engineered conduits (decellularized,
bioresorbable) to reduce reintervention
burden.

name: Acquired Pulmonary Vein Stenosis
description: Progressive stenosis of one or more pulmonary veins occurring after surgical repair of TAPVR, or arising de novo in premature infants without prior surgery. Distinct from congenital pulmonary vein disease (TAPVR, #17). The post-surgical form is one of the most challenging conditions in pediatric interventional cardiology: stenosis is highly aggressive in young infants, often multivessel, and recurs rapidly (50- 70% restenosis within months). Carries very high mortality without successful intervention.

frequency.us: ~200–500 US total clinically significant acquired PVS cases
frequency.sources: Clinically significant acquired PV stenosis after TAPVR repair in ~10–20% of patients

diagnosis: Echo: reduced or absent flow in affected pulmonary veins; elevated left atrial pressure. Cardiac MRI or CT angiography: delineates PV anatomy, degree of stenosis, and multivessel disease. Cardiac catheterization + selective PV angiography: gold standard for stenosis severity and anatomy. Lung perfusion scan (V/Q): quantifies differential blood flow. Wedge angiography technique for distal stenosis visualization.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Transcatheter balloon PV angioplasty.
Drug-eluting balloon (paclitaxel-coated):
improving short-term results over plain
balloon. Sutureless PV liberation surgery:
creates wider, pericardium-lined pathway.
Lung transplantation for severe bilateral
disease not amenable to other interventions.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Sirolimus (systemic mTOR
inhibitor): active trials at Boston Children's
and Nationwide Children's — anti-
proliferative effect on myofibroblast-driven
stenosis; most promising emerging therapy.
Drug-eluting stents (sirolimus-eluting) for in- stent restenosis. Imatinib + bevacizumab

name: Coronary Artery Fistula
description: Congenital anomalous communication between a coronary artery and a cardiac chamber (coronary-cameral fistula: most commonly to RV or RA) or a vascular structure (coronary-arteriovenous fistula: most commonly to pulmonary artery). Causes volume loading of the drainage chamber, myocardial ischemia (coronary steal), and risk of bacterial endocarditis.

frequency.us: rupture (rare). US: ~360–720 US total (0.1–0.2% of CHD)
frequency.sources: Coronary artery fistula ~0.1– 0.2% of CHD; majority discovered incidentally

diagnosis: Echo: turbulent flow jet entering cardiac chamber or pulmonary artery; dilated coronary artery. CT coronary angiography: gold standard for anatomy, fistula tract, drainage site. Cardiac catheterization + selective coronary angiography: fistula tract anatomy, Qp/Qs measurement, branch vessel assessment before embolization. Stress testing for ischemia (large fistulas with steal).

treatment.standardOfCare:
Transcatheter embolization: preferred
for suitable anatomy — coil embolization
(detachable/pushable) for small-to-medium
fistulas; Amplatzer Vascular Plug for large-
diameter fistulas. Technical priority: preserve
feeding coronary branches. Surgical ligation
for anatomy not amenable to catheter
closure. Observation for small asymptomatic
fistulas. SBE prophylaxis post-closure.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Covered stent exclusion for large
fistulas as an alternative to embolization. CT
coronary angiography for pre-procedural
mapping and post-closure surveillance.
Multimodality imaging (FFR, IVUS) to
assess hemodynamic significance of small
fistulas.

diagnosis: Clinical presentation: progressive cyanosis after initially adequate Glenn palliation, without echocardiographic evidence of shunting. Contrast echo: microbubbles appear in left heart after peripheral venous injection without passing through the heart (pulmonary A-V passage) -- diagnostic. CT pulmonary angiography: visualizes PAVM locations. Cardiac MRI: differential lung blood flow. Cardiac catheterization: pulmonary vein saturation step- downs; selective pulmonary angiography.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Fontan completion — definitive treatment; restoration of hepatic venous blood flow reverses PAVMs in most cases (regression typically 3–12 months post- Fontan). Transcatheter embolization for large discrete accessible PAVMs (temporizing). Hepatic vein inclusion in
Fontan pathway is critical for anatomical
variants with hepatic vein exclusion.
treatment.emerging:
Emerging:Hepatic vein flow redistribution:
catheter-based selective hepatic venous
redirection as bridge to Fontan completion.
Understanding of hepatic factor biology
(identity of anti-PAVM hepatic factor) under
active investigation — may lead to
pharmaceutical approaches.

name: Kawasaki Giant Coronary Aneurysm with Stenosis  TIER 3 — DEFINING: The cardiac condition IS a germline syndrome or near-universally caused by an identified genetic mutation TIER
description: Distinct, late-phase complication of Kawasaki disease characterized by progressive stenosis within or adjacent to giant coronary artery aneurysms (Z-score >=10 or absolute diameter >=8mm). Stenosis results from myofibroblast proliferation and organized thrombus within the aneurysm. Causes myocardial ischemia, MI, and sudden cardiac death. Distinct from acute Kawasaki disease (#79): requires interventional coronary management rather than anti-inflammatory treatment.
diagnosis: Coronary angiography (catheterization): gold standard for anatomy and stenosis severity. CT coronary angiography: non-invasive surveillance (annual or biannual). Stress imaging (nuclear perfusion, stress MRI, dobutamine stress echo): ischemia assessment. IVUS and OCT: assess aneurysm wall, thrombus, and stenosis anatomy -- critical for intervention planning. Echo: aneurysm size follow-up, LV wall motion.

treatment.standardOfCare:
Lifelong anticoagulation: warfarin +
low-dose aspirin for giant aneurysms (z-
score ≥10). PCI: balloon angioplasty ±
rotational atherectomy (calcified lesions) +
drug-eluting stents preferred. CABG: for
multivessel or PCI-unsuitable disease —
internal mammary artery conduits preferred
(avoid saphenous vein in young patients).
Thrombolytics or catheter-directed aspiration
for acute coronary occlusion.
